ocd-bill/0f429223-7646-4873-aa7c-b5eb112.summary: AB 1170 is California's annual code maintenance bill. It makes nonsubstantive technical changes across various code provisions to carry out the Legislative Counsel's recommendations for maintaining the codes. It was signed and chaptered as Chapter 67, Statutes of 2025, on July 28, 2025.
mechanics: Implements the existing statutory duty of the Legislative Counsel to advise the Legislature on legislation needed to maintain the codes.
Makes only nonsubstantive changes, such as corrections, conforming edits and cleanup, according to the official abstract.
Affects unspecified 'various provisions of the law'. The full text was not available, so the specific code sections amended cannot be confirmed here.
Enacted as Chapter 67, Statutes of 2025, chaptered 2025-07-28.
ocd-bill/0f429223-7646-4873-aa7c-b5eb112.comparison: No comparable bills from other states were listed. This is a routine housekeeping vehicle rather than a gaming policy bill, and it is unusual only in that it may touch many code sections at once without changing their legal effect.
ocd-bill/0f429223-7646-4873-aa7c-b5eb112.watch: Check the chaptered text to see whether any technical edits land in Penal Code gambling provisions, the Gambling Control Act (Bus. & Prof. Code §19800 et seq.) or horse-racing wagering statutes, so that compliance citations and internal references stay accurate.

ocd-bill/0ba2a530-5bea-413a-9386-e3a34cb.summary: HB 4155 is Arizona's FY2026-2027 amusements budget reconciliation bill. It folds the fantasy sports contest fund (repealing ARS 5-1212) and the unarmed combat subaccount (moved out of the racing regulation fund) into the event wagering fund under ARS 5-1318. It also lets the Department of Gaming spend up to $500,000 a year of its event wagering regulatory share on problem gambling grants. It imposes a one-year 0.5% regulatory assessment on pari-mutuel handle and temporarily relaxes first-time starter rules for racehorses.
mechanics: Secs. 5-6: Fantasy sports fees (up to 10% of adjusted revenues) and late-payment penalties (5% per month, capped at 25%) are now deposited in the event wagering fund. ARS 5-1212 is repealed and remaining fantasy sports fund balances transfer to that fund.

Sec. 7 (ARS 5-1318): The event wagering fee cap (10% of adjusted gross event wagering receipts, benchmarked to the highest tribal compact revenue share), the operator's choice of cash or modified accrual accounting, and the due date (the 25th of the following month) are left in place. The fund now also receives fantasy sports monies, and 90% of monthly deposits still sweep to the general fund.

Sec. 7: The department's 10% regulatory spending authority now covers both chapter 10 (fantasy sports) and event wagering. Of that 10%, up to $500,000 per fiscal year may support problem gambling programs, and new subsection E allows grants funded from these monies plus private donations, grants or federal funds.

Secs. 2-4, 7: An unarmed combat subaccount is created in the event wagering fund. Boxing gross receipts tax (4%), license fees and withheld purses are redirected there, and the department may transfer its enforcement costs into the subaccount from the event wagering fund.

Sec. 8: For FY2026-2027 only, commercial racing permittees owe a regulatory assessment of 0.5% of amounts wagered on live and simulcast races, in-state and out-of-state. It is payable from pari-mutuel pool deductions on top of the takeout allowed under ARS 5-111(B).

Sec. 9: For 2026-2027 race meetings, first-time starters may race with gate approval and two timed workouts, one of them out of the gate within 60 days of the race. This provision is repealed after December 31, 2027. Sec. 1 separately changes the liquor licenses fund reversion to monies over $700,000 on December 31 of each year.
ocd-bill/0ba2a530-5bea-413a-9386-e3a34cb.comparison: No other states' bills were provided for comparison. What stands out is that Arizona is using event wagering fund infrastructure, which was built on sportsbook fees, to absorb unrelated regulatory programs: fantasy sports, boxing and MMA oversight, and problem gambling grants. It does this without changing the operator fee cap. The bill also continues a one-year pari-mutuel regulatory assessment that is stacked on top of statutory takeout.
ocd-bill/0ba2a530-5bea-413a-9386-e3a34cb.watch: Watch whether consolidating fantasy sports, unarmed combat and problem gambling costs into the event wagering fund pressures the Department of Gaming to raise the event wagering fee toward the 10% cap in ARS 5-1318(A), or to justify larger regulatory transfers out of operator-generated revenue.

ocd-bill/0a4c88eb-a987-4653-9f3d-2a4e520.summary: SB 1671 continues the Arizona Department of Gaming, which regulates tribal gaming, fantasy sports and event wagering, only until July 1, 2028, while continuing the Arizona Racing Commission and the Boxing and MMA Commission until July 1, 2032. It adds annual conflict-of-interest disclosure requirements for agency staff and requires a public complaint intake and tracking system. It also directs the Department to review independent audits back to 2021 to determine whether event wagering operators paid the correct privilege fees under A.R.S. 5-1318, and to correct any overpayments or underpayments under its rules.
mechanics: Sunset: new A.R.S. 41-3028.11 terminates the Department of Gaming on July 1, 2028 and repeals 5-601 through 5-604 and Title 5, chapters 10 (fantasy sports) and 11 (event wagering) on January 1, 2029. The racing and boxing/MMA commissions run to July 1, 2032 (41-3032.11, 41-3032.15). Sections 5 and 6 apply retroactively from July 1, 2026.

Privilege fee true-up (Sec. 10): the Department must review all independent audits conducted as of 2021 to check whether event wagering operators paid the correct privilege fee under 5-1318, and must address overpayments and underpayments 'as required by rule.'

Complaints (new 5-606): the Department must post a complaint submission process on its website covering chapters 2, 6, 10 and 11. It must report annually to the Senate President, House Speaker and Governor on complaints received, dismissed and resolved.

Conflict of interest (5-101.01(G), 5-223(E), 5-604(E)): directors, deputies, commissioners and employees must file a disclosure form on appointment or hire, and an updated form annually if their information changes. Under 5-101.01(H), failure to comply is grounds for dismissal.
Audit reporting (5-604(F)): by December 17 each year, the Department must submit all third-party audits of the Department to legislative leaders and the Governor.
Sec. 7 states the continuation purposes: tribal compact oversight under IGRA, fantasy sports integrity, event wagering enforcement, and regulation of racing and combat sports.
ocd-bill/0a4c88eb-a987-4653-9f3d-2a4e520.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. Unusually, this is a sunset-review continuation that does more than reauthorize the agency. It gives the gaming regulator only a two-year extension, against six years for the sibling commissions, which forces a near-term legislative revisit of event wagering law. It also mandates a retroactive multi-year audit of operator privilege fee payments.
ocd-bill/0a4c88eb-a987-4653-9f3d-2a4e520.watch: Operators should watch for (1) Sec. 10 privilege fee reconciliation reaching back to 2021, which could produce assessments for underpayments, and the rules governing how corrections are made; and (2) the July 1, 2028 sunset of the Department and repeal of chapter 11 effective January 1, 2029, which opens event wagering law to renegotiation in the 2028 continuation bill. Analysis is based on the introduced text, so the enacted version may differ.

ocd-bill/0c552149-6d28-45bd-aefa-904d17f.summary: AB 831 (Chapter 623, Statutes of 2025) makes it a misdemeanor to operate, conduct, or offer an online sweepstakes game in California. It also makes it a crime for payment processors, financial institutions, geolocation providers, gaming content suppliers, platform providers, and media affiliates to knowingly and willfully support or promote one. It also expands California's existing unfair-practices rules for contests and sweepstakes so they expressly reach internet websites and online apps, and it redefines simulated gambling to include examples such as lottery games, bingo, and sports wagering.
mechanics: Unfair-practice expansion: the existing ban on electronic simulated-gambling methods tied to sweepstakes prizes now expressly covers 'any method, including an internet website or an online application.' The term 'gambling-themed games' is deleted, and 'gambling' is redefined to include examples such as lottery games, bingo, sports wagering, or any game that mimics or simulates similar gambling.

Payment-system trigger: it is an unfair practice to offer such games using a payment system that lets a person play a simulated gambling program for direct or indirect consideration, with eligibility for a prize, cash or cash equivalents, or a chance to win them. This applies in a business establishment, on the internet, or via an online app. Games that do not award cash prizes or cash equivalents are expressly not made unlawful.
New crime: it is unlawful for any person or entity to operate, conduct, or offer an online sweepstakes game (as defined in the bill) in California.

Secondary liability: any entity, financial institution, payment processor, geolocation provider, gaming content supplier, platform provider, or media affiliate that knowingly and willfully supports, directly or indirectly, the operation, conduct, or promotion of an online sweepstakes game in the state is also liable.
Penalties: misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $1,000 to $25,000, up to one year in county jail, or both. The bill creates a state-mandated local program with no reimbursement required.

Carve-outs: lawful games and methods of gambling enterprises licensed under the Gambling Control Act, and California State Lottery operations, are exempt. So are limited, occasional promotional sweepstakes by for-profit businesses that are incidental to substantial bona fide sales of consumer products or services and are not a vehicle for ongoing gambling.
ocd-bill/0c552149-6d28-45bd-aefa-904d17f.comparison: The closest analogue on the list is AR HB 1861, which makes operating an illegal online casino or sports betting a felony within a broader interactive gaming framework. AB 831 is narrower in target (online sweepstakes games) and lighter in penalty (misdemeanor), but it reaches further down the supply chain by naming payment processors, geolocation vendors, content suppliers, platforms, and media affiliates. Unlike GA HB 686, HI HB 2570, and HI HB 1308, which would legalize and tax sports wagering, AB 831 authorizes nothing; it is purely prohibitive. KY HB 904, by contrast, regulates rather than bans an adjacent contest product (fantasy contests).
ocd-bill/0c552149-6d28-45bd-aefa-904d17f.watch: Watch the 'knowingly and willfully' secondary-liability clause and the express inclusion of sports wagering in the simulated-gambling definition, because vendors, payment partners, and media affiliates that also serve sweepstakes-model or prize-based sports products face misdemeanor exposure in California, where sports betting remains unlicensed and the exemption covers only Gambling Control Act licensees and the State Lottery.

ocd-bill/1c33d2a1-7bd1-4570-83d4-18d5a71.summary: SSB 1240 (renumbered SF 660) appropriates a total of $22 million from Iowa's sports wagering receipts fund (Code section 8.57I) for FY 2025-2026: $14 million to the Department of Education for an education support personnel pay supplement distributed to school districts by enrollment, and $8 million to the Department of Public Safety for the public safety equipment fund. It does not change sports wagering tax rates, licensing, or operator obligations.
mechanics: Sec. 1: $14,000,000 from the sports wagering receipts fund to the Department of Education for FY 2025-2026 to supplement compensation of education support personnel, defined as regular and part-time non-salaried school district employees.

Each district's share equals $14,000,000 multiplied by its FY 2024-25 budget enrollment divided by the statewide total budget enrollment. Districts must report support-personnel data to the department on or before July 1, 2025 to qualify.
The funds are treated as miscellaneous income under section 257.2, are excluded from district cost computations under chapter 257, and are paid on the foundation aid schedule under section 257.16.
Sec. 2: $8,000,000 from the same fund to the Department of Public Safety for deposit in the public safety equipment fund (section 80.48).
Sec. 3: the education appropriation takes effect upon enactment. The public safety appropriation follows the normal effective date.
Per the explanation, the fund is fed by the internet fantasy sports contest tax (Code 99E.6) and the sports wagering net receipts tax (Code 99F.11(5)).
ocd-bill/1c33d2a1-7bd1-4570-83d4-18d5a71.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. The bill is a routine appropriation of existing sports wagering and fantasy sports tax revenue. It is notable mainly because it earmarks wagering receipts for non-gaming purposes (school support staff pay and police equipment) rather than for problem-gambling or regulatory programs, and it leaves the underlying tax structure untouched.
ocd-bill/1c33d2a1-7bd1-4570-83d4-18d5a71.watch: Operators face no direct new obligations here, but growing legislative reliance on sports wagering receipts for recurring education and public safety spending could build pressure to raise the 99F.11 net receipts tax rate in future sessions.

ocd-bill/17b7a400-0d6d-4b77-aef1-a80bed1.summary: HB 686 (House Higher Education Committee substitute, LC 56 0648S) would legalize online-only sports betting in Georgia, with the Georgia Lottery Corporation acting as both regulator and "master sports betting licensee." It caps the market at 16 Type 1 licenses, most tied to Georgia pro teams and sports venues, and imposes a 27.5% privilege tax on adjusted gross income, with proceeds going to a dedicated trust fund for the constitutionally specified purposes. The bill has a contingent effective date tied to Georgia constitutional provisions, and it died after being reported favorably by substitute on 2026-03-06.
mechanics: Market structure (50-27-133): no more than 16 Type 1 licenses. Five are reserved for qualifying Georgia pro teams (baseball, football, men's and women's basketball, soccer). One each goes to a 30-year PGA-tour tournament body, a 30-year invitational golf facility, a NASCAR track owner, and the Lottery Corporation. The remaining seven go to online sports betting services providers through public procurement. Each eligible entity may contract with only one platform provider, and entities must give notice of intent within 60 days or be permanently disqualified.

Tax (50-27-150): 27.5% annual privilege tax on adjusted gross income, paid monthly by the services provider. AGI is wagers minus federal excise tax minus winnings paid, including the cash value of merchandise. Negative AGI may be carried forward. The tax is in lieu of other state and local taxes and fees on sports betting operations or proceeds, and it is deposited quarterly into the Georgia Sports Betting Proceeds Trust Fund.

Fees and terms (50-27-130, -131): Type 1 licenses carry a $100,000 application fee and a $1M annual fee. Services provider licenses are $10,000/$100,000, and supplier licenses are $2,000/$20,000. Licenses run five years. Operators must hold a reserve of at least $500,000 or their outstanding wager liabilities, whichever is greater. Operators licensed elsewhere may receive temporary licenses for up to one year.

Launch timing: Lottery rules are due within 90 days, exempt from the Georgia APA. Applications for all 16 licenses open on the same date, and timely applicants get a common go-live date no later than July 31, 2027. No Type 1 licensee may launch until at least one procurement-based provider is licensed.

Wagering scope: bettors must be 21 or older and physically present in Georgia. Wagers covered include in-play, parlay, props and exchange wagering. Proposition bets on collegiate sporting events are banned (50-27-135). Youth events with mostly under-18 participants and Special Olympics are excluded. Official league data is defined for settling tier 2 wagers, but the operative mandate falls in the truncated portion of the text.

Regulatory limits and carve-outs: the corporation may not set hold or payout percentages (50-27-123(b)). Leagues and Type 1 eligible entities may sign revenue-share agreements without corporation approval (50-27-131(d)). Institutional investors are exempt from qualification requirements. The corporation must set responsible gaming rules covering self-exclusion (SSN required), bet limits for problem gamblers, 1-800-GAMBLER notices and advertising guidelines aimed at minors.
ocd-bill/17b7a400-0d6d-4b77-aef1-a80bed1.comparison: Like HI HB 2570 and HI HB 1308, HB 686 creates a full licensing regime from scratch. Hawaii places regulation in DBEDT or the Department of Law Enforcement and taxes through a general excise tax on operator licenses. Georgia instead uses its lottery corporation as regulator and operator, with a team- and venue-tethered cap of 16 licenses. Georgia's 27.5% GGR rate sits well above Colorado's 10% rate (whose deductions CO HB 25-1311 narrows) and is in the range of higher-tax states like Louisiana after LA HB 639. Unlike CO SB 131, Georgia leaves deposit and bet limits to rulemaking rather than fixing statutory caps.
ocd-bill/17b7a400-0d6d-4b77-aef1-a80bed1.watch: Watch three things: the scarcity of the seven procurement-based skins and the one-platform-per-Type-1-entity rule; the 27.5% rate, where the only promotional relief is the merchandise-as-winnings language in the AGI definition; and the truncated official league data provisions for tier 2 wagers, which could impose data-purchase costs.

ocd-bill/1a61fc8c-7649-4386-a076-d02aaf7.summary: SB 25-107 is a routine Colorado supplemental appropriation that amends the FY 2024-25 Department of Revenue line items in the Long Bill (HB 24-1430, Part XX). It also extends the spending authority for $1.6 million of FY 2022-23 money appropriated in HB 23-1017 so it remains available through the end of FY 2024-25. It makes no change to sports betting or gaming law, rates, or licensing. The Limited Gaming Division and Sports Betting Fund figures appear only as restated, informational appropriation lines.
mechanics: The only visible change in Section 1 cuts the Executive Director's Office 'Payments to OIT' line from $22,016,901 to $21,431,378, a reduction of $585,523 in cash funds. Cash funds for that line fall from $10,540,215 to $9,954,692, and 'various sources of cash funds' fall from $49,201,661 to $48,616,138.
Part XX total cash funds drop from $358,439,946 to $357,854,423.

The Limited Gaming Division is restated at $44,980,060 and 106.0 FTE. This includes $1,755,188 from the Sports Betting Fund (§ 44-30-1509(1)(a), C.R.S.), shown 'for informational purposes only' because that fund is continuously appropriated. It also includes $26,035,153 for distributions to gaming cities and counties and $3,200,000 for the Responsible Gaming Grant Program from its cash fund (§ 44-30-1702(8)(a)).
Section 2 amends HB 23-1017 so that $1,600,000 of unexpended money from section (1)(C) of that act stays available until the close of FY 2024-25 for the same purpose.
Section 3 is a safety clause, so the act took effect immediately on the Governor's signature on 2025-02-27.
ocd-bill/1a61fc8c-7649-4386-a076-d02aaf7.comparison: Unlike substantive gaming bills such as GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570, which would authorize and license sports wagering, SB 25-107 creates no regulatory or licensing framework. Unlike LA HB 639, which changes online sports wagering tax rates, and IA SF 605, SSB 1152 and HSB 91 on withholding from winnings, it does not touch tax rates, withholding, or revenue dedication. It is closest to omnibus appropriation bills like IA HSB 343 and IA SSB 3199. Gaming appears only as departmental budget lines, and even the Sports Betting Fund line is non-binding and informational.
ocd-bill/1a61fc8c-7649-4386-a076-d02aaf7.watch: Nothing in the bill affects operator obligations, though the restated Sports Betting Fund ($1,755,188) and Responsible Gaming Grant ($3.2 million) lines are a useful baseline for tracking Division of Gaming regulatory spending against sports betting tax receipts in later Long Bill or supplemental cycles.

ocd-bill/22c69e46-ba07-4e5c-82d5-3c8234e.summary: HB 373 amends Alabama's Entertainment Industry Incentive Act of 2009. It renames the Alabama Film Office the Alabama Entertainment Office, adds music albums as a qualified production with their own spend thresholds, and raises the per-project rebate ceiling and the annual program cap. It also reserves part of the cap for music albums and allows limited carryover of unspent incentives. Wagering appears only in an existing exclusion from the definition of qualified production, which the bill leaves unchanged.
mechanics: §41-7A-43(a): the rebate stays at 25% of non-resident-payroll production expenditures plus 35% of Alabama-resident payroll, with a $500,000 project minimum. The per-project expenditure ceiling rises from $20 million to $25 million.
New §41-7A-43(f): music-album-only projects qualify if they spend at least $30,000, with no rebate on spending above $200,000.
§41-7A-48(a): the aggregate annual cap rises from $20 million to $30 million starting with the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026.

§41-7A-48(b)-(c): $2 million of the cap is reserved for music albums until July 1 each year, after which it is released to other productions. Up to $3 million in unspent incentives may carry forward each fiscal year.

§41-7A-42(8)b: the existing exclusion of sporting events, in-house corporate advertising, and 'any form of gambling, gaming, wagering, or pari-mutuel wagering activity or enterprise' from 'qualified production' is retained unchanged.
Effective October 1, 2025.
ocd-bill/22c69e46-ba07-4e5c-82d5-3c8234e.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. On its own, the bill is a film and music incentive expansion. Its only contact with gaming is the carried-over exclusion in §41-7A-42(8)b barring gambling or wagering enterprises and sporting-event productions from the rebate. The music-album reserve with a July 1 release date is the bill's novel feature.
ocd-bill/22c69e46-ba07-4e5c-82d5-3c8234e.watch: Operators should note that Alabama's rebate program continues to exclude gambling and wagering activity or enterprises, sporting-event productions, and in-house corporate advertising, so betting-related content or commercials produced in Alabama are unlikely to qualify for the expanded $30 million incentive pool.

ocd-bill/2baf55e1-b90f-49ac-a668-4a11417.summary: SB 253 amends Alabama's Entertainment Industry Incentive Act of 2009 to add a small-production rebate of 45 percent of Alabama-resident payroll for projects with $100,000 to $499,999 in production expenditures, funded from an optional $2 million annual reserve. It also tightens when payments to loan-out companies count toward the rebate, lowers thresholds for soundtrack and music video projects, and pushes the outside program evaluation deadline to the 2028 Regular Session. Gambling appears only in the existing definition of 'qualified production', which continues to exclude any form of gambling, gaming, wagering or pari-mutuel activity, along with sporting events.
mechanics: New §41-7A-43(b): the office may reserve up to $2,000,000 a year for small-budget productions. These earn a 45 percent rebate on Alabama-resident payroll if total production expenditures fall between $100,000 and $499,999. The existing program stays at 25 percent of non-resident-payroll expenditures plus 35 percent of resident payroll, with a $500,000 minimum and a $20 million per-project ceiling.

§41-7A-42(6) and (7)d: loan-out company payments count as payroll or production expenditures only if the production company withheld and remitted Alabama tax at the highest rate (§40-18-71 withholding, or §40-18-5/§40-18-31 income tax). That withholding satisfies the loan-out company's estimated and composite tax obligations.
Soundtrack projects: minimum drops from $50,000 to $30,000 and the cap from $300,000 to $200,000. Music video minimum drops from $50,000 to $30,000.
Existing §41-7A-42(8)b, unchanged: the definition of qualified production excludes sporting events and any form of gambling, gaming, wagering or pari-mutuel wagering activity or enterprise.

The aggregate cap stays at $22 million from FY2026, with $2 million reserved for music albums and carryover limited to $3 million. The 'department' definition switches from Commerce to Revenue, the Commerce-contracted out-of-state evaluation is now due on the first legislative day of the 2028 session, and the program sunset remains December 31, 2028.
Effective October 1, 2026.
ocd-bill/2baf55e1-b90f-49ac-a668-4a11417.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. This is a film and entertainment tax-incentive bill. Its only gaming touchpoint is a pre-existing carve-out that keeps gambling, wagering and sporting-event content out of the rebate program; SB 253 does not amend that carve-out.
ocd-bill/2baf55e1-b90f-49ac-a668-4a11417.watch: Note that §41-7A-42(8)b continues to bar gambling, wagering and sporting-event productions, so sportsbook-produced commercials, branded content or betting-related digital media could not claim the expanded 45 percent small-production rebate or the sales, use and lodging tax exemptions.

ocd-bill/383e0365-b0bc-4df2-94fc-814805e.summary: Illinois Senate Resolution 1319 is a memorial resolution mourning the death of George Francis Dietz. Based on the official abstract (the full text is unavailable), it is purely commemorative and has no regulatory, tax, or gaming content. The Senate adopted it on 2025-01-07.
mechanics: Expresses the Senate's condolences on the death of George Francis Dietz.
Non-binding Senate resolution with no statutory effect, rates, thresholds, definitions, or enforcement provisions.
Adopted by the Illinois Senate on 2025-01-07; single-chamber resolutions do not go to the other chamber or the Governor.
ocd-bill/383e0365-b0bc-4df2-94fc-814805e.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed, and none would be expected for a memorial resolution. The only unusual thing about it is that it appeared in a sports-betting or gaming search at all, most likely through keyword or subject-index matching rather than anything in its substance. The abstract does not mention wagering or gaming, so even the 'incidental' rating overstates its relevance.
ocd-bill/383e0365-b0bc-4df2-94fc-814805e.watch: Nothing to watch for operators, since this is a ceremonial memorial with no gaming provisions; it can be removed from the tracking list unless the full text shows some unexpected link to the industry.

ocd-bill/2ebd542f-e3f7-4bb6-84f0-fe60410.summary: Iowa's DIAL agency bill, renumbered SF 2289, includes a gambling division that gives the Racing and Gaming Commission express power to issue cease and desist orders and seek injunctions against anyone offering pari-mutuel or advance deposit wagering, internet fantasy sports, games of chance, sports wagering, or illegal sweepstakes in Iowa without a commission license or other legal authorization. It also extends the existing lifetime exclusion for class D felony cheating offenses, and for two unlawful-betting convictions, to sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering. The other two divisions cover unrelated building code and residential care facility housekeeping.
mechanics: Sec. 1 (99D.5(4)): removes the $30,000-per-year total cap on expense reimbursement for Racing and Gaming Commission members; the $10,000 annual salary is unchanged.

Secs. 2–4 (99D.7(25), 99E.3(2)(f), 99F.4(13)): add express cease-and-desist and injunctive-relief authority against unlicensed pari-mutuel/ADW operators, unlicensed internet fantasy sports contest operators, and anyone offering games of chance, gambling, sports wagering, or 'illegal sweepstakes' without a commission license or specific legal authorization.

Sec. 5 (99F.15(4)): a person who commits the listed class D felony offenses is barred for life from sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering (as defined in 99F.9), not just from excursion gambling boats and gambling structures.
Sec. 6 (99F.15(6)(c)): two convictions for unlawful betting trigger the same lifetime bar, now covering sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering.

Divisions II–III: building code fees are redirected to the licensing and regulation fund (10A.507), safe-room rules are to be developed with Homeland Security and Emergency Management, and pediatric palliative residential care facilities may serve zero individuals. These are not gaming-related.
Status: SSB 3040 was approved in committee on 2026-02-11 and renumbered SF 2289; no separate effective date is stated, so the standard July 1 default would apply.
ocd-bill/2ebd542f-e3f7-4bb6-84f0-fe60410.comparison: Unlike the comprehensive authorization bills listed, GA HB 686 and HI HB 2570/HB 1308, this bill assumes an existing Iowa sports wagering market and only sharpens enforcement and exclusion tools. Its swipe at 'illegal sweepstakes' through regulator injunctive power parallels the anti-sweepstakes focus of CA AB 831 and CA SB 451, but it works by expanding agency authority rather than defining prohibited sweepstakes conduct. It is closer in spirit to regulator-housekeeping bills like CO SB 163 and KY HB 566 than to the consumer-protection limits in CO SB 131.
ocd-bill/2ebd542f-e3f7-4bb6-84f0-fe60410.watch: Watch how the commission uses its new cease-and-desist and injunction authority under 99F.4(13) against sweepstakes, social casino, prediction-market, or other offshore and unlicensed offerings, since the undefined phrases 'illegal sweepstakes' and 'otherwise being specifically authorized by law' will set the reach of that authority. Licensed operators should also update their exclusion-list compliance for the expanded lifetime bans from sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering.

ocd-bill/42b34b3a-ef76-4d16-91c1-f449117.summary: SF 605 amends Iowa Code section 99F.18 to declare that all winnings from sports wagering authorized under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax, with any state tax withheld remitted to the Department of Revenue on the winner's behalf. It also amends section 422.16(2)(d) to require state income tax withholding on sports wagering winnings whenever federal withholding is required on the same winnings under the Internal Revenue Code. The Act takes effect January 1, 2026.
mechanics: Sec. 1 splits 99F.18 into two subsections: subsection 1 keeps the existing rule for slot machine winnings, and new subsection 2 extends the same earned-income treatment and remittance duty to sports wagering winnings under chapter 99F.

Sec. 2 adds a state withholding trigger for chapter 99F sports wagering that is tied to the federal trigger. State tax must be withheld whenever the Internal Revenue Code requires federal withholding on the same winnings, rather than at a fixed dollar threshold.
Existing state withholding thresholds are unchanged: winnings over $600 under chapters 99B and 99G, over $1,000 under chapter 99D, and over $1,200 for slot machines under chapter 99F.
Operators must remit amounts withheld under 422.16(2) to the Iowa Department of Revenue on behalf of the winner.
Sec. 3 makes the Act effective January 1, 2026. It was signed by the Governor on March 28, 2025.
ocd-bill/42b34b3a-ef76-4d16-91c1-f449117.comparison: Unlike the operator-side tax measures listed, SF 605 addresses only bettor-level income tax withholding and does not touch the operator tax rate or how it is calculated. Those operator-side measures are LA HB 639, which changes the online sports wagering tax, and CO HB 25-1311, which limits deductions from net sports betting proceeds. It also differs from the comprehensive authorization bills, GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570, which create licensing and tax frameworks from scratch. What is unusual is that Iowa ties state withholding to the federal trigger instead of setting its own dollar threshold, so the state obligation will move automatically with any change to federal withholding rules.
ocd-bill/42b34b3a-ef76-4d16-91c1-f449117.watch: Operators should update payout and withholding systems before January 1, 2026 so that Iowa withholding is triggered in lockstep with federal withholding on sports wagering winnings. They should also watch for Department of Revenue guidance on the withholding rate, remittance timing, and how federal threshold changes flow through.

ocd-bill/2f147010-c67a-4a40-b54e-bbd8f37.summary: SB 1681 would require the Arizona Department of Gaming to issue an event wagering operator license to every federally recognized Arizona tribe that has signed the current gaming compact. It appears to remove the existing ten-license cap on tribal licenses and to let tribal licensees offer retail sportsbooks near sports facilities, not just mobile wagering. It would also strip confidentiality from licensing application materials and expand the department's annual reporting on the 2021 compact trust fund.
mechanics: Sec. 2, A.R.S. 5-1304(A): the department 'shall' issue a license to each compacted federally recognized tribe on application, replacing the permissive cap of not more than ten tribal licenses. The ten-license limit for non-tribal applicants (sports team owners, PGA tour facility operators, NASCAR promoters or their designees) appears to remain.

5-1304(A)(2) and (D): tribes, tribally owned entities or their contracted designees may offer both mobile wagering statewide and retail wagering within a five-block radius of a sports facility or complex. This deletes the current restriction to mobile-only wagering outside Indian lands. A designee is treated as the applicant. Retail facilities may sit in retail or commercial space on non-Indian land, and the existing one-mile/quarter-mile rule for facilities near tribal casinos is retained.

Sec. 3, A.R.S. 5-1305(H): reverses confidentiality. The department 'may not' keep application and investigation records, interviews, reports and financial data confidential. It must release them immediately to any legislator on written request, and they are not exempt from court orders, subpoenas, audits or Arizona public records law (title 39, ch. 1, art. 2).
5-1305(F): the exemption from state licensure is limited to tribes operating event wagering exclusively on Indian lands; on-reservation wagering remains governed by the compact and IGRA.

Sec. 1, A.R.S. 5-605(E): the annual 2021 compact trust fund report is due within ninety days after fiscal year end instead of by September 30. It must be separate from other department reports, signed by the director, copied to the Secretary of State, and itemize the following: quarterly balances, eligibility calculations, deposits by contributing tribe, line-item expenditures, disbursements by tribe and date, and administrative draws by the department.
No specific effective date or new fees or tax rates appear in the text; licenses remain five-year terms with annual fees under 5-1310.
ocd-bill/2f147010-c67a-4a40-b54e-bbd8f37.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. The bill is unusual on its own for combining three things: converting a capped, discretionary tribal license allocation into a mandatory entitlement for every compacted tribe, giving tribal licensees off-reservation retail rights near sports venues that Arizona's 2021 framework reserved to professional sports franchises, and making operator application files publicly disclosable. That last element runs opposite to the confidentiality protections most state sports-betting statutes provide.
ocd-bill/2f147010-c67a-4a40-b54e-bbd8f37.watch: Operators should watch the 5-1305(H) confidentiality reversal, which would expose financial statements, bankroll data, ownership details and background materials to public records requests and legislators. They should also watch the expansion of tribal licenses with retail rights near stadiums, which could dilute the limited market and the exclusivity sports-franchise licensees currently hold and could reopen compact negotiations.

ocd-bill/3bd11053-a171-4b09-ae4e-ca7209a.summary: SF 465 is an omnibus agency bill for the Iowa Economic Development Authority (IEDA) and the Iowa Finance Authority. It restructures review committees, repeals the brownfield redevelopment program and council, and tightens and retimes the historic preservation tax credit. It also replaces the title guaranty board with a division under the IFA board and consolidates arts and culture programs into a new arts and culture enhancement fund. Its only gaming touchpoint is Sec. 36, which redirects part of an existing annual appropriation out of Iowa's casino wagering tax distribution statute (Code 99F.11) into that new fund.
mechanics: Sec. 36 amends Code 99F.11(4)(d)(1). The $520,000 annual appropriation to IEDA from gambling tax distributions stays the same, and half still goes to operational support grants. The other half moves from the community cultural grants program into the new arts and culture enhancement fund (Code 15.436, rewritten by Sec. 32). Neither the amount nor any wagering tax rate changes.

Division IV (Secs. 14-15) changes the review committees for the community attraction and tourism program (15F.203) and the sports tourism marketing and infrastructure program (15F.402). The IEDA director will appoint members 'with relevant expertise' instead of the committee being five IEDA board members. These are tourism grant programs, not sports wagering.

Division III (Secs. 11-13) repeals 15F.106, which required recipients of both Vision Iowa and community attraction and tourism (CAT) assistance to pay at least 50% of employee health insurance. The repeal applies prospectively and retroactively to prior awards.

Division V tightens the historic preservation tax credit. It excludes single-family dwellings unless the project creates two or more new units (Sec. 17), and resets the commencement and completion deadlines to run from the registration date, with up to 12-month extensions (Sec. 19). It also allows the authority to exceed the $45 million annual award cap by up to 20% for projects generating credits of $10 million or more, with the excess counted against the next year's cap (Sec. 21).

Division II repeals 15.292-15.295 (the brownfield redevelopment program, fund and advisory council), transfers the fund's remaining money, and replaces the CPA audit with an investor-commissioned CPA examination. Division VIII repeals the Great Places, cultural trust and related sections (Sec. 37) and sweeps their balances into the arts and culture enhancement fund (Sec. 38).
ocd-bill/3bd11053-a171-4b09-ae4e-ca7209a.comparison: Unlike the sports-betting authorization bills such as GA HB 686, HI HB 1308 and HI HB 2570, or the operator-conduct bills such as CO SB 131 and KY HB 904, SF 465 does not regulate wagering at all. The nearest analogues are LA HB 639 and CO HB 25-1311, which change how gaming revenue is taxed or dedicated. LA HB 639 changes online sports wagering and video poker tax rates and dedicates gaming revenue. CO HB 25-1311 narrows deductions from net sports betting proceeds. SF 465 only re-labels the destination of one existing $520,000 slice of 99F.11 gaming tax money, without touching any rate or deduction; its tourism focus is closer to FL HB 7031's tourist development tax changes than to any gaming bill.
ocd-bill/3bd11053-a171-4b09-ae4e-ca7209a.watch: Operators can largely ignore this bill (now renumbered SF 622), but should monitor whether later amendments use the 99F.11 distribution provision in Sec. 36 to reopen wagering tax allocations or add new earmarks from gaming revenue.

ocd-bill/43f8bf91-5164-494b-84b6-f3e01b8.summary: H 4615 is the House-engrossed fiscal year 2025 supplemental budget. It mainly makes supplemental appropriations, including about $2.05 billion for MassHealth fee-for-service, and makes assorted changes to health-care fund, pension, vaccine and licensing law. In the portion of the text provided, its only gaming-related change is Section 10, which lets the State Lottery Commission contract for new lottery games on a revenue-share basis outside the appropriation process.
mechanics: Section 10 amends G.L. c.10 §25. The Lottery Commission may enter contracts or group agreements for lottery games 'not currently or previously authorized by the commission'. The contractor or licensor may be paid a specified percentage of net or gross game revenue, and those payments are not subject to appropriation.

Section 11 creates G.L. c.23A §13W, a non-budgeted Sports and Entertainment Events Fund run by the Office of Travel and Tourism. It funds competitive grants for major sports and entertainment events, with no single recipient receiving more than half the fund balance in a calendar year. Grantees must make labor-compliance, procurement and apprenticeship certifications, and the Attorney General enforces them.
Section 2A item 1595-0605 transfers $15,000,000 to that fund, of which at least $10,000,000 is reserved for 2026 World Cup matches hosted in Massachusetts.
The bill carries an emergency preamble, so it takes effect immediately on enactment. Supplemental sums remain available through June 30, 2026.
The provided text is truncated at about page 29 of 124, so any further gaming provisions later in the bill cannot be confirmed.
ocd-bill/43f8bf91-5164-494b-84b6-f3e01b8.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. What stands out is that Massachusetts is using a must-pass supplemental budget to quietly widen Lottery Commission contracting authority. The authority covers revenue-share deals for new game types and keeps vendor payments off-budget, which could ease the procurement of new products such as digital lottery games without standalone legislation.
ocd-bill/43f8bf91-5164-494b-84b6-f3e01b8.watch: Watch whether Section 10's open-ended authority for 'lottery games not currently or previously authorized' survives the House-Senate conference (the bill was reported in part by H4761) and is later used to procure online or iLottery products that would compete with licensed sports-wagering operators for consumer spend.

ocd-bill/47562725-ee45-4bec-8140-b79365c.summary: SF 395 makes proxy betting and account sharing on Iowa-licensed gambling and sports-wagering platforms a form of criminal illegal gaming under Iowa Code section 725.7. It also adds chapters 99E and 99F to the exceptions in that section and extends the paid wager-delivery offense to items received outside a gambling structure. Penalties follow the existing illegal-gaming ladder, from a serious misdemeanor up to a class C felony, depending on the amount involved and prior offenses.
mechanics: Sec. 1 adds two definitions to section 99F.1. "Account sharing" (new subsection 01) means agreeing between two or more persons to share access, temporarily or permanently, to a licensee account for gambling games or sports wagering, for the purpose of concealing a person's identity. "Proxy betting" (new subsection 25A) means one person placing a wager for another with intent to hide the bettor's identity, and it expressly includes requesting another person to do so.
Sec. 2 adds section 99F.15(3A), which states that a person engaging in proxy betting or account sharing violates section 725.7.

Sec. 3 amends section 725.7(1). It adds new paragraphs f (proxy betting) and g (account sharing) to the list of illegal-gaming acts. It also widens the lead-in exception from chapters 99B and 99D to chapters 99B, 99D, 99E and 99F, and adds 99E and 99F to the bookmaking exception in paragraph e.

Sec. 3 also amends paragraph d so that, for a fee, delivering anything of value received outside a 99D racetrack enclosure or outside a gambling structure, to be placed in a pari-mutuel pool or other authorized wagering system, is illegal gaming.

Penalties are tiered by amount and are unchanged by the bill. Fourth degree ($100 or less) starts at a serious misdemeanor and rises to a class C felony on a fourth offense. First degree (over $5,000) is a class C felony, punishable by up to 10 years and a fine of $1,370 to $13,660.
No effective date or operator-specific duties are stated in the text.
ocd-bill/47562725-ee45-4bec-8140-b79365c.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. On its own, SF 395 is unusual in criminalizing the bettor's conduct directly rather than imposing know-your-customer or account-integrity duties on operators. Its proxy-betting definition is broad: it covers 'any wagering or betting activity', not only activity with a licensee, and reaches anyone who merely requests that another place a bet. Account sharing is tied to 99F licensee accounts and requires a purpose of concealing identity.
ocd-bill/47562725-ee45-4bec-8140-b79365c.watch: Watch whether the felony-level exposure for proxy betting and account sharing will prompt the Racing and Gaming Commission or prosecutors to expect operators to detect and report shared or proxy accounts, and how the new 'except as permitted in chapter 99F' lead-in interacts with paragraphs f and g, given the bill passed the Senate but was rereferred to House Public Safety on 2025-05-15.

ocd-bill/4c8cbcd1-fae5-4e43-839f-8827411.summary: HR 826 is a ceremonial Georgia House resolution recognizing and commending Atlanta multimedia personality Rashan Ali Smith for her radio, sports broadcasting, television and community work, including founding the nonprofit Sporty Girls, Inc. It creates no legal obligations and contains nothing on sports betting, gaming or wagering.
mechanics: The resolving clause (lines 33-35) has the House recognize and commend Rashan Ali Smith and extend best wishes; it carries no statutory or regulatory effect.
The second resolving clause (lines 36-38) directs the House Clerk to make a copy of the resolution available to Ms. Smith.
The recitals cover her career as a sports anchor (Headline News, CNN), CBS Sports Network sideline reporter, radio host, and co-host of TV One's Sister Circle Live.
The recitals note that Sporty Girls, Inc., founded in 2006, has served nearly 2,000 Metro Atlanta girls and is planned to relaunch in 2025.
Status: read and adopted by the House on 2025-03-27; as a single-chamber resolution it needs no further action.
ocd-bill/4c8cbcd1-fae5-4e43-839f-8827411.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed, and none would be expected, because this is a purely honorific resolution. Its only connection to the gaming practice area is the honoree's background in sports media. It does not reference wagering, operators, taxation, advertising or licensing.
ocd-bill/4c8cbcd1-fae5-4e43-839f-8827411.watch: Nothing to watch for operators: the resolution has no regulatory content and can be excluded from sports-betting tracking, though it may have been flagged on sports-related keywords.

ocd-bill/4b1ccced-2c68-485c-b4b6-34c0688.summary: As filed, HB 7031 is a general sales tax rate-reduction bill that cuts Florida's state sales and use tax from 6 percent to 5.25 percent and makes matching cuts across chapter 212, including transient rentals, admissions, commercial real property rentals and coin-operated amusement machines. It touches gaming only incidentally, by lowering the tax on charges for coin-operated amusement machines and on admissions. This analysis covers the filed text; the bill was later enacted as Chapter 2025-208 and may have been substantially amended before passage, so check the enrolled version.
mechanics: Section 5 amends s. 212.05(1) to cut the general sales, use and rental rate on tangible personal property from 6 percent to 5.25 percent, and the electricity rate from 4.35 percent to 3.6 percent. Section 1 makes the matching change to the combined electricity rate in s. 203.0011, from 6.95 percent to 6.2 percent.

Section 5 amends s. 212.05(1)(h) to cut the tax on charges for coin-operated amusement machines from 4 percent to 3.25 percent. Gross-receipts divisors are reset (for example, 1.04 becomes 1.0325 in counties with no surtax), while the $30-per-machine identifying certificate fee and the $250-per-machine penalty are left unchanged.

Section 4 amends s. 212.04 to cut the admissions tax from 6 percent to 5.25 percent; the existing exemptions for major sporting events (NFL championship, FIFA World Cup, Formula One, Daytona 500 and others) are retained.

Sections 2 and 3 cut the transient rentals and parking/dock/storage rate in s. 212.03 to 5.25 percent, and the commercial real property rental (business rent) tax in s. 212.031 from 2.0 percent to 1.25 percent.
The title authorizes the Department of Revenue to adopt emergency rules and provides effective dates; the specific dates fall in the truncated portion of the text and are not shown.
ocd-bill/4b1ccced-2c68-485c-b4b6-34c0688.comparison: Unlike CO HB 25-1311, which limits deductions in calculating net sports betting proceeds, and LA HB 639, which changes the tax on online sports wagering, FL HB 7031 does not touch any wagering tax base or rate. It also does not address withholding on winnings, as IA SF 605, IA SSB 1152 and IA HSB 91 do. Its only gaming-adjacent elements are the lower rates on coin-operated amusement machine receipts and admissions, so it is closer to general revenue packages such as KY HB 757 or AZ SB 1274 than to the sports-betting bills listed.
ocd-bill/4b1ccced-2c68-485c-b4b6-34c0688.watch: Operators should confirm from the enrolled Chapter 2025-208 which rate cuts actually took effect and when, especially the admissions, business rent and coin-operated amusement machine rates that affect venue, retail and arcade-style operations, since the filed text may not match the final law.

ocd-bill/4d1307a3-4913-42ae-92e2-f9230f1.summary: SF 613 (renumbered SF 625 on 2025-04-16) raises Iowa's sports wagering tax on net receipts from 6.75% to 9%. It flattens the casino adjusted gross receipts (AGR) tax by eliminating the lower graduated tiers, and doubles the per-capacity casino license fee. It also stops passing DCI gaming enforcement costs through regulatory fees, funding them instead from AGR tax revenue, and redirects sports wagering receipts to public safety equipment and a new $15 million major events and tourism fund.
mechanics: Sec. 18 amends 99F.11(5)(a) to raise the sports wagering net receipts tax from 6.75% to 9%. Division I takes effect January 1, 2026 (Sec. 19), mid-fiscal year.

Secs. 14-15 replace the graduated AGR schedule (5% on the first $1M, 10% on the next $2M, then 22% to 24%) with a flat rate on all AGR: 22% for excursion boats and gambling structures, and 24.120% for racetrack enclosures regardless of table games license. Promotional play receipts are taxed by reference to the new subsection 1 rate (Sec. 16).

Sec. 9 raises the annual excursion boat and gambling structure license fee from $5 to $10 per person capacity. Secs. 3-5 and 10-13 strike the DCI enforcement cost component, and the related revolving fund deposits, from 99D.14 and 99F.10 regulatory fees. Sec. 17 instead credits AGR tax to the gaming enforcement revolving fund up to the DPS appropriation, starting FY2026-27. The 99E.4(4) fantasy sports background check fees are untouched.

Sec. 1 appropriates $8 million annually from the sports wagering receipts fund to the public safety equipment fund (80.48) starting FY2026-27. Sec. 24 appropriates $15 million from the same fund in FY2025-26 to the new Iowa major events and tourism fund (ch. 15G).

Secs. 6 and 8 route simulcast horse race tax revenue to a new Iowa horse racing fund (99D.27B). The commission distributes it to entities regulated under the federal Horseracing Integrity and Safety Act, with reversion to the rebuild Iowa infrastructure fund if HISA is repealed.

Divisions II-III create the major events grant program, which requires a 50% match and caps administrative use at 5%. They also repeal the sports tourism marketing program fund (15F.403), transfer its balance to the new fund, and open sports tourism infrastructure grants to any nonprofit organization.
ocd-bill/4d1307a3-4913-42ae-92e2-f9230f1.comparison: Like LA HB 639, which raises taxes on online sports wagering and dedicates gaming revenue, SF 613 pairs a sports wagering rate hike with earmarks. Iowa's resulting 9% rate would still be low nationally, and Iowa also restructures the land-based casino AGR tax in the same bill. CO HB 25-1311 targets the deductions used to compute the taxable base rather than the headline rate, whereas Iowa leaves its net receipts definition alone. HI HB 1308/HB 2570 and GA HB 686 would build new sports wagering regimes from scratch, while SF 613 adjusts an existing market's rates, fees and revenue uses.
ocd-bill/4d1307a3-4913-42ae-92e2-f9230f1.watch: Watch whether the 9% rate survives the renumbered SF 625 and how a January 1, 2026 effective date is applied to a tax imposed on net receipts 'each fiscal year,' including proration and whether any promotional deduction changes are added later.

ocd-bill/5f99305a-3821-44ad-a384-989f4cc.summary: Act 494 gives Louisiana's gaming regulators (the Gaming Control Board and State Police gaming enforcement division, the Racing Commission, the Office of Charitable Gaming, and the Lottery Corporation via the gaming enforcement division) express statutory authority to obtain state and FBI fingerprint-based criminal history record information on applicants, licensees, permittees, and employees. Under the Gaming Control Board's Title 27 jurisdiction, which expressly includes the Louisiana Sports Wagering Act and Fantasy Sports Contests Act, every license or permit applicant and every person required to be found suitable must now submit a full set of fingerprints for a national check. The Act takes effect August 1, 2026.
mechanics: New R.S. 27:15(B)(1)(b) requires every applicant for a license or permit, and any person required to be found suitable under Title 27, to submit fingerprints to the gaming enforcement division, which forwards them to the FBI. The board and the division are the designated recipients of the results.

New R.S. 27:20.1 defines 'criminal history record information' to include state arrest, prosecution, and conviction records, including those expunged or dismissed under Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 893 and 894, plus national fingerprint-based records. The definition of 'permit' covers any permit, license, or authorization, or associated application, issued under Title 27.

Use of fingerprints is limited to eligibility determinations under the suitability standards in R.S. 27:28, 234, 235, 306, 427, and 604. The records are confidential under R.S. 27:21 and may be used exclusively to evaluate eligibility or disqualification. They are also available to the board and the Louisiana Department of Justice.

The bureau's costs under R.S. 15:587, including the costs of the FBI check, may be imposed on the individual. Under amended R.S. 47:9065(B), the bureau may charge the Lottery Corporation or the applicant a reasonable processing fee.

Parallel sections are added for the Racing Commission (R.S. 4:147.3, tied to R.S. 4:150 suitability) and the Office of Charitable Gaming (R.S. 4:705.1). R.S. 15:587(C) is rewritten to route state and FBI results to each agency.
Under new R.S. 47:9065(C), the gaming enforcement division may share criminal history results with the Lottery Corporation to determine eligibility of vendors, retailers, and employees.
ocd-bill/5f99305a-3821-44ad-a384-989f4cc.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. On its own, the Act is unusual in two respects. It is a cross-agency housekeeping statute that recodifies express FBI fingerprint-check authority for every Louisiana gaming regulator at once. It also explicitly sweeps expunged and Article 893/894 dismissed records into what regulators may review, rather than changing any substantive licensing standard, tax, or operating rule.
ocd-bill/5f99305a-3821-44ad-a384-989f4cc.watch: Operators should watch how the board applies the new mandatory fingerprinting of 'any person required to be found suitable', which could extend to key persons, owners, vendors, and employees of sports wagering and fantasy licensees, along with the review of expunged or dismissed records and the pass-through of check fees to individuals.

ocd-bill/5db4da54-f598-48bf-9222-022f67e.summary: SF 2085 creates a new Iowa Code chapter 99H requiring CFTC-regulated designated contract markets (prediction markets) to obtain a Department of Revenue permit before offering event-driven contracts in Iowa, and imposes a 20% tax on their Iowa-apportioned adjusted revenues. It also decouples Iowa individual and corporate income tax from IRC section 1256 for event-driven contracts, so trader gains are taxed in a gambling-like way with losses capped at 90% of gains. It requires state withholding on gains over $600. The bill was approved in committee on 2026-03-12 and renumbered as SF 2470.
mechanics: Covered contracts (99H.1(6)): fixed binary-payout derivatives traded on a CFTC-regulated designated contract market, limited to sporting activities, elections, legislative actions and economic indicators. Chapter 99D pari-mutuel wagering, chapter 99E fantasy sports and chapter 99F sports wagering are excluded (99H.3).

Permit (99H.4): no person may serve as a designated contract market at a place of business in Iowa or through delivery sales without a Department of Revenue permit. The initial fee is $10 million, and the annual renewal fee is $100,000. Permits expire each June 30.

Tax (99H.5): 20% of adjusted revenues. Adjusted revenues are total charges and fees collected from all traders in a contract, less payouts, multiplied by the Iowa 'location percentage' (the share of the contract's fees collected from Iowa traders). All proceeds go to the general fund (99H.6).

Income tax (Secs. 8 and 10, amending 422.7 and 422.35): IRC section 1256 treatment does not apply to event-driven contracts. Taxpayers must back out section 1256 net gain or loss and add back gross gains. Itemizers may subtract losses only up to 90% of the gains added back.

Withholding (Sec. 9, 422.16(2)): state withholding applies to section 1256 event-contract gains over $600. Under 99H.7, payouts are deemed Iowa earned income, and the contract market must remit withheld amounts.

Retroactivity (Sec. 11): the income tax changes apply retroactively to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. Sec. 11 cites '422.33, subsection 15', but Sec. 10 actually amends 422.35, which looks like a drafting error.
ocd-bill/5db4da54-f598-48bf-9222-022f67e.comparison: Unlike the conventional sports-wagering authorization bills listed (GA HB 686, HI HB 2570 and HB 1308) and the sportsbook tax measures (LA HB 639, CO HB 25-1311), SF 2085 does not regulate sportsbooks at all. Instead it targets CFTC-regulated prediction markets with a revenue-agency tax-and-permit regime, with no gaming-regulator licensing, suitability or integrity rules. Its 20% rate and $10 million entry fee far exceed Iowa's own chapter 99F sports wagering framework, which the bill expressly carves out. Its income tax decoupling from section 1256, with the 90% loss cap, is an unusual feature not found in any of the listed bills.
ocd-bill/5db4da54-f598-48bf-9222-022f67e.watch: Watch whether the renumbered SF 2470 keeps the 20% rate and $10 million fee, whether a permit implicitly legitimizes sports event contracts competing with 99F licensees without equivalent regulatory oversight, and whether the scheme survives CFTC preemption challenges, including the 422.33/422.35 drafting error in the retroactivity clause.

ocd-bill/61da2c80-cf50-496a-b7f4-7ceb59b.summary: SB 1847 is Arizona's FY2026-27 general appropriations act, signed June 13, 2026. It amends the FY2025-26 Department of Corrections appropriation (Laws 2025, ch. 233, sec. 23) and makes FY2026-27 agency appropriations. The excerpt provided runs through Sec. 13 (Attorney General) and contains no gaming, wagering or sports-betting provisions.
mechanics: Sec. 1 revises the FY2025-26 Department of Corrections appropriation to a total of $1,600,697,200, raising the operating lump sum to $828,190,500 and cutting the private prison per diem and inmate health care lines.
Sec. 2 limits spending to the listed funding sources and bars backfilling from other sources if a listed source is unavailable.
Sec. 5 appropriates $299,933,300 to the Department of Administration, including county distributions such as $10,000,000 in Gila County disaster relief and $7,000,000 in county sheriff support.
Sec. 10 sets AHCCCS at $22,960,437,700 total ($2,919,510,700 from the state general fund), with $51,500,000 for Public Law 119-21 Medicaid implementation.
Sec. 13 appropriates $106,604,400 to the Attorney General, including $16,918,400 from the consumer protection-consumer fraud revolving fund.
This is the introduced version; the enacted text may differ, and the excerpt is truncated before any Department of Gaming section.
ocd-bill/61da2c80-cf50-496a-b7f4-7ceb59b.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. Arizona's general appropriations acts typically carry a Department of Gaming section, but that portion is not in the supplied excerpt, so no gaming-related appropriations, fund transfers or event-wagering provisions can be confirmed from this text.
ocd-bill/61da2c80-cf50-496a-b7f4-7ceb59b.watch: Get the enacted chaptered version and check the Department of Gaming section and any fund sweeps for changes to regulatory funding, event wagering fund appropriations or problem-gambling allocations, none of which appear in the excerpt provided.

ocd-bill/5fd28bb2-732d-4e93-aef3-29d7da5.summary: SB 1801 rewrites A.R.S. 5-1314(F) so event wagering operators may use official, nonofficial or alternative league data to settle tier two (in-game and prop-type) sports wagers, apparently removing Arizona's current rule that operators must use official league data once a league offers it. It also requires official league data to be unbundled and sold league by league or sport by sport. Section 1 reprints and renumbers the 5-1301 definitions. Because strike-through formatting is lost in the extracted text, the exact deletions are uncertain, including whether the standalone definition of "official league data" survives.
mechanics: Sec. 2, 5-1314(F): an event wagering operator "may use official league data, nonofficial league data or alternative league data" for tier two sports wagers.

The existing exclusive-use mandate appears to be struck. That mandate requires official data once a league or its authorized entity opts to provide it, unless the operator shows the department the feed is not available on commercially reasonable terms.
Anti-bundling rule: official league data "shall not be bundled." The league, its authorized entity or a data provider must list, price, offer, lease and sell data separately by league or sport.
Operators may buy data for a single league or sport and cannot be required to buy fixed-price, multi-league or sport-menu packages.

Sec. 1, 5-1301: definitions are renumbered. The text shows tier one wagers (final score or outcome only, placed before the event starts) and tier two wagers (all others), and "wager" is defined to include both. The "official league data" entry (old para. 9) appears without a new number, suggesting it may be repealed even though 5-1314(F) still uses the term.

No new effective date, penalty or enforcement mechanism appears. The existing free-bet and promotional-credit deduction schedule in the adjusted gross receipts definition is reprinted, but the text does not show whether it is changed.
ocd-bill/5fd28bb2-732d-4e93-aef3-29d7da5.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. On its own, the bill is unusual because it goes beyond simply repealing an official league data mandate. It also imposes affirmative anti-bundling and per-league sale obligations on leagues and data distributors, regulating the supply side of the data market. Most official-data fights involve only whether operators must buy league data, not how leagues must package and price it.
ocd-bill/5fd28bb2-732d-4e93-aef3-29d7da5.watch: Confirm against the formatted enrolled text exactly what is struck, especially the official league data definition and any free-bet deduction language, and expect league and data-distributor opposition to the anti-bundling mandate, including whether the department gains any rulemaking or enforcement authority over data pricing.

ocd-bill/657ee32e-a8af-4230-aaaa-983c86d.summary: SF 622 (renumbered SF 642 on 2025-04-23) is an omnibus Iowa Economic Development Authority and Iowa Finance Authority bill that restructures program governance, repeals the brownfield program and several arts and culture programs, and amends the historic preservation tax credit. Its only gaming-related provision, Sec. 39, redirects part of an existing $520,000 annual appropriation drawn from Chapter 99F gambling revenues into a newly reconstituted arts and culture enhancement fund. Nothing in the bill touches sports wagering authorization, licensing, tax rates or operator conduct.
mechanics: Sec. 39 amends Code section 99F.11(4)(d)(1) so that the half of the $520,000 annual appropriation to IEDA previously earmarked for the community cultural grants program is instead deposited in the arts and culture enhancement fund under rewritten section 15.436. The other half stays with operational support grants.

Sec. 35 rewrites section 15.436 to create the arts and culture enhancement fund, which is non-reverting and keeps its interest. Sec. 41 sweeps unobligated balances from the Iowa great places fund, the Iowa cultural trust fund and the cultural trust grant account into it, and Sec. 40 repeals sections 15.437 to 15.441 and 15.476 to 15.482.

Division II repeals the brownfield redevelopment program, fund and advisory council (sections 15.292 to 15.295). It also replaces the required CPA audit for redevelopment tax credits with a CPA attestation examination plus a statement of final qualifying investment.

Division V amends the historic preservation tax credit. It bars eligible taxpayers from transferring certificates on or after January 1, 2026, and makes credits 100% refundable for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. It ties the commencement deadline to one year and the completion deadline to three years from the registration date, and allows the $45 million annual cap to be exceeded by up to 20% for projects generating credits of $10 million or more.

Divisions III and IV repeal section 15F.106 on required benefits, with retroactive applicability, and shift review of community attraction and tourism and sports tourism marketing applications to director-appointed five-member committees. Division VII eliminates the title guaranty board.
Division X raises the Iowa Reinvestment Act district size cap from 75 to 125 acres for districts approved on or after July 1, 2020, retroactive to that date.
ocd-bill/657ee32e-a8af-4230-aaaa-983c86d.comparison: Unlike the sports-wagering bills listed (GA HB 686, HI HB 1308 and HB 2570, CO HB 25-1311, CO SB 131), SF 622 does not regulate, license or tax wagering. Its only gaming link is a redirection of an existing fixed appropriation sourced from Chapter 99F revenues. The closest analogue is LA HB 639, which also dedicates gaming revenues, but LA HB 639 changes online sports wagering and video poker tax rates, while SF 622 leaves rates untouched. Like FL HB 7031, it is primarily a tourism and tax-credit vehicle, and its sports tourism provisions concern marketing grants rather than betting.
ocd-bill/657ee32e-a8af-4230-aaaa-983c86d.watch: Watch whether later versions of SF 642 expand the Sec. 39 reallocation of 99F.11 gambling revenue or attach other claims on wagering-tax proceeds, since omnibus economic-development bills are a common vehicle for re-dedicating gaming revenue streams.

ocd-bill/62320026-16df-4452-8504-f2c6a85.summary: SB 1667 amends Arizona's event wagering chapter (A.R.S. 5-1301, 5-1314) and the lottery statute (5-554) to add e-sports to the definition of sports event, tighten the definition of "other event" so it excludes online casino-style games, and appears to repeal the official league data mandate for in-game (tier two) wagers. Because the introduced text as provided does not show strikethrough or underlining, which language is added and which is deleted has to be inferred from the renumbering; it should be confirmed against the official version.
mechanics: 5-1301: adds a new definition of "e-sport event" (an organized, multiplayer video game competition, particularly between professional players, individually or as teams) and adds e-sport events to the definition of "sports event" alongside professional, collegiate, motor race and Olympic events.

5-1301 and 5-554: "other event" means a competition of relative skill or an event authorized by the Department of Gaming. It expressly excludes any internet or mobile electronic game whose interface depicts spinning reels or replicates slots, blackjack, poker, roulette, craps or other casino-style games. In the lottery statute, the cross-reference to 5-1301 is replaced with this standalone definition.

5-1301: the renumbering indicates the definitions of "official league data," "tier one sports wager" and "tier two sports wager" are deleted, and the tier references in the "wager" definition appear to be removed. Section 5-1314(F), which requires operators to use official league data for tier two wagers unless it is not available on commercially reasonable terms and bars bundling, is amended and appears to be repealed or narrowed.

5-1301(1): the promotional-credit deduction schedule (20% in years 1-2, 15% in year 3, 10% in years 4-5, none from year 6) is pegged to April 15, 2021 rather than to "the effective date of this section." The January 1 start-year rule and the 20% pre-start deduction remain in the text.
Integrity definitions are extended to other events: "prohibited conduct" and "prohibited participant" cover manipulation of other events and of individual occurrences or performances within them.

5-554: the lottery may not base noncomputerized draw outcomes on any sports event or other event. The conditional trigger language in 5-554(J) for the keno and mobile draw games appears to be removed.
ocd-bill/62320026-16df-4452-8504-f2c6a85.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. On its own, the bill is unusual in pairing an expansion of the wagering menu (e-sports) with an apparent rollback of Arizona's official league data requirement, one of the few such mandates in the country. It also writes an anti-iGaming carve-out directly into the definition of "other event."
ocd-bill/62320026-16df-4452-8504-f2c6a85.watch: Confirm against the official strikethrough version whether 5-1314(F) and the official league data and tier definitions are actually repealed, since that would end the leagues' leverage over in-play data pricing, and check whether the casino-style exclusion in "other event" could be read to limit novel event markets.

ocd-bill/6ae19381-66be-48e8-a9ed-b3a4389.summary: Kentucky SB 3 rewrites the state's college name, image, and likeness statute (KRS 164.6941 to 164.6951) so that institutions and their affiliated corporations may pay student-athletes directly through written institutional agreements, including revenue sharing permitted or required by a legal settlement. It replaces the old prevailing market rate test with a prevailing range of compensation standard, and removes the prior bans on institutional NIL payments and on NIL inducements tied to recruiting. It keeps the ban on student-athletes endorsing sports betting and took effect immediately under an emergency clause.
mechanics: Section 3(4)(a): a student-athlete may not enter an NIL agreement with a third party for the endorsement or promotion of sports betting. The same list bars controlled substances, association-banned substances, adult entertainment, and products illegal for the athlete to possess.

Section 3(2)-(3): institutions or affiliated corporations (newly defined by reference to KRS 164A.610) may pay athletes under institutional agreements. They may also designate a media rights holder or other third parties with whom athletes may contract directly for NIL deals.

Section 1(15): the new 'prevailing range of compensation' standard requires a valid business purpose tied to promoting goods or services sold to the public, at rates comparable to similarly situated athletes not at the institution.

Section 4(2): athletes must submit proposed third-party NIL agreements to the institution, which has up to 3 business days to identify conflicts. Section 4(7) exempts these agreements from the Open Records Act.

Section 6: institutional, NIL, and agency contracts for athletes at Kentucky institutions are governed by Kentucky law. Agreements must be reaffirmed within 30 days of the athlete turning 18 or leaving the program.
Section 8: emergency clause, so the act was effective on signature, March 13, 2025 (Acts Ch. 10).
ocd-bill/6ae19381-66be-48e8-a9ed-b3a4389.comparison: Like LA HB 513 and HI HB 2384, this is an NIL statute that accommodates institutional payments and revenue sharing; the only wagering content is the sports-betting endorsement ban in Section 3(4)(a). AR HB 1861 goes the other way by folding NIL into gaming regulation, treating NIL-based games as interactive gaming. That contrasts with Kentucky's approach of walling NIL off from betting promotion. None of the sports wagering authorization bills listed (GA HB 686, HI HB 1308/2570, KS SB 356) address athlete endorsement deals in this way.
ocd-bill/6ae19381-66be-48e8-a9ed-b3a4389.watch: Operators and their marketing affiliates cannot sign Kentucky college athletes to endorsement or promotional deals, including through any third party an institution designates under Section 3(3), and institutional review under Section 4(2) will screen for this.

ocd-bill/6e9bf409-74c0-4e5e-a2fb-b29a932.summary: SB 1499 amends A.R.S. 5-1202 (fantasy sports) and 5-1304 (event wagering) to expand and firm up fingerprint-based state and federal criminal background checks run through the Department of Gaming. It requires DPS to pass fingerprint data to the FBI, which it previously only "may" do. It also lets the Department require fingerprints from employees, contractors, management companies, holding companies and suppliers, including ancillary suppliers, and expressly authorizes the Department to receive the resulting state and federal criminal history records.
mechanics: 5-1202(E): fantasy sports applicants' officers, directors, members, partners, principals and individual owners of 10% or more must submit full fingerprint sets to the Department of Gaming for checks under 41-1750 and Public Law 92-544. The Department forwards the data to DPS, and DPS "shall" (no longer "may") exchange it with the FBI.

New 5-1202(H)–(I): the Department may require fingerprints from fantasy contest operator employees, contractors, management companies, holding companies and suppliers, including ancillary suppliers, and is authorized to receive the resulting criminal records. Existing subsections are relettered J–L, with two-year licenses and biennial renewal unchanged.

5-1304(B)(2): the event wagering fingerprint requirement is restated so that the Department exchanges data with DPS and DPS "shall" exchange it with the FBI. Fingerprints still come from officers and directors (corporations), members (LLCs) and partners (partnerships), and a disqualifying conviction still bars licensure.

New 5-1304(E)–(F): the Department may require fingerprints from employees and contractors of event wagering operators and designees, limited event wagering operators, management services providers and event wagering suppliers, including ancillary suppliers, and may receive the resulting state and federal records.

The bill leaves untouched the event wagering license cap (10 non-tribal and 10 tribal), the five-year license term, the one-license-per-person rule and the fee structure; subsections are simply relettered (G, H). The text also appears to make a minor wording change to the designee language in 5-1304(D)(1).
No effective date or penalty provisions are added. Status: introduced, Senate second reading on 2025-03-31.
ocd-bill/6e9bf409-74c0-4e5e-a2fb-b29a932.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. On its own, the bill is a narrow technical fix to Arizona's licensing statutes rather than a policy change. Its explicit statutory authorization for fingerprint-based FBI checks and for the Department's receipt of the records is the kind of language the FBI requires under Public Law 92-544 before it will release criminal history to a state agency. Its notable reach is the extension of potential fingerprinting to rank-and-file employees, contractors and ancillary suppliers across both fantasy and event wagering.
ocd-bill/6e9bf409-74c0-4e5e-a2fb-b29a932.watch: Watch how the Department uses its new discretionary power to fingerprint employees, contractors, management services providers and ancillary suppliers. Broad application could add compliance cost, onboarding delays and disqualification risk for vendors and staff who were not previously screened.

ocd-bill/71571cd4-cbf0-434f-a5bb-d46aec6.summary: SB 1777 amends the definition of "other event" in Arizona's event wagering chapter (A.R.S. 5-1301) and the lottery statute (5-554). Under the new definition, an "other event" is a competition of relative skill or an event authorized by the Department of Gaming, but it expressly excludes any internet or mobile electronic game whose interface depicts spinning reels or replicates a slot machine, blackjack, poker, roulette, craps or another casino-style game. The bill also adds Indian tribes and entities fully owned by an Indian tribe to the definition of "person" and makes conforming and technical edits, including pinning the free-bet deduction schedule to April 15, 2021.
mechanics: 5-1301(12): "Other event" means a competition of relative skill or an event authorized by the Department of Gaming under chapter 13. It excludes online or mobile electronic games with a user interface that depicts spinning reels or replicates slots, blackjack, poker, roulette, craps or any other casino-style game.

5-554(P)(9): The lottery statute replaces its cross-reference to 5-1301 with a standalone, identical "other event" definition (cross-referencing chapter 11). This keeps the bar on lottery draw methods that depend on sports events or other events.

5-1301(13): "Person" expressly includes an Indian tribe or an entity fully owned by an Indian tribe. This matters for licensee and event wagering operator status, since tribes may hold mobile event wagering licenses under 5-1301(7)(b).
