5-1301(1): The free-bet and promotional-credit deduction from adjusted gross event wagering receipts is tied to April 15, 2021 rather than "the effective date of this section." The tiered caps (20% in years 1–2, 15% in year 3, 10% in years 4–5) are unchanged.

5-554(B)(2) and (J): The text references gaming conducted under the 2021 tribal-state compact amendments and the keno and mobile draw authorization. Because the introduced version's strike and insert formatting is not legible here, it is unclear which language is new and which is deleted.
Definitions are renumbered within 5-1301. There is no new tax rate, penalty or effective-date provision beyond the general effective date.
ocd-bill/71571cd4-cbf0-434f-a5bb-d46aec6.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. What is unusual is that the bill uses a definitional carve-out, rather than a standalone prohibition, to keep casino-style online games from being authorized as "other events" under Arizona's event wagering chapter. That protects tribal compact exclusivity over casino gaming. It also explicitly brings tribes and tribally owned entities within "person."
ocd-bill/71571cd4-cbf0-434f-a5bb-d46aec6.watch: Watch whether the casino-style user-interface exclusion in the "other event" definition is applied by the Department of Gaming to narrow novel products (such as gamified, skill-based or micro-event wagering markets) that operators offer or plan to offer under the event wagering license.

ocd-bill/74d58a78-7a5d-44af-b656-98326d3.summary: H 4601 is the House Ways and Means version of the Massachusetts FY2025 supplemental budget, totalling about $2.26 billion, most of it ($2.05 billion) for MassHealth fee-for-service payments, plus a range of unrelated statutory changes. Its only gaming-related provision is Section 10, which lets the State Lottery Commission contract for new lottery games on a revenue-share basis without appropriation. It also creates a Sports and Entertainment Events grant fund, which does not touch wagering.
mechanics: Section 10 amends G.L. c. 10, s. 25 so the lottery commission may enter contracts or group agreements for lottery games "not currently or previously authorized by the commission." The contractor or licensor may be paid a specified percentage of net or gross revenues of the game, and those payments are not subject to appropriation.

Section 11 creates G.L. c. 23A, s. 13W, a non-budgeted Sports and Entertainment Events Fund run by the Office of Travel and Tourism. It funds competitive grants for major sports or entertainment events, with no single recipient getting more than half the fund balance in a calendar year. Grantees face labor, procurement and apprenticeship certifications, enforced by the Attorney General, and an annual report is due January 1.
Item 1595-0605 transfers $15,000,000 to the new fund, of which at least $10,000,000 is for costs of 2026 World Cup matches hosted in Massachusetts.
The bill carries an emergency preamble, so it takes effect on enactment. Supplemental sums are available through June 30, 2026.
The text supplied is truncated at roughly page 30 of 99, so later sections have not been reviewed.
Last action, 2025-10-15: published as amended (see H4615). The operative version may differ from this text.
ocd-bill/74d58a78-7a5d-44af-b656-98326d3.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. What stands out is that Section 10 sits inside a supplemental budget yet broadly authorizes the Lottery Commission to launch and outsource new game types on uncapped, off-budget revenue-share terms. That is a procurement and appropriation change that could make new lottery products easier to stand up without separate enabling legislation. It does not amend the sports wagering statute (G.L. c. 23N) or address operator taxes, licensing or advertising.
ocd-bill/74d58a78-7a5d-44af-b656-98326d3.watch: Watch whether Section 10's authority for "lottery games not currently or previously authorized" survives in H4615 and the final enactment, and whether the Lottery uses it for online or draw-style products that could compete with or overlap licensed sports wagering under c. 23N; also check the unreviewed remaining pages for any c. 23K or c. 23N amendments.

ocd-bill/897c73d6-df17-4716-9742-f18ad0d.summary: Iowa SSB 1152, a Department of Revenue bill later renumbered SF 605, amends Code section 99F.18 to declare that all winnings from sports wagering authorized under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax. It amends section 422.16(2)(d) to require Iowa income tax withholding on sports wagering winnings whenever federal withholding is required on the same winnings under the Internal Revenue Code. Amounts withheld must be remitted to the Department of Revenue on the winner's behalf.
mechanics: Sec. 1 adds new subsection 2 to Iowa Code 99F.18. It states that all sports wagering winnings under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax laws.

Sec. 1 also requires that amounts deducted from sports wagering winnings under 422.16(2) be remitted to the Department of Revenue on behalf of the winner, mirroring the existing slot machine rule in 99F.18(1).

Sec. 2 amends 422.16(2)(d) to tie the state withholding trigger for sports wagering to the federal trigger. Under IRC rules this is generally winnings over $5,000 that are at least 300 times the wager.
The existing withholding thresholds stay the same: $600 for chapter 99B and 99G (lottery) winnings, $1,000 for chapter 99D (pari-mutuel) winnings, and $1,200 for chapter 99F slot machines.
The bill sets no state withholding rate; the rate is governed by existing 422.16.
Sec. 3 makes the Act effective January 1, 2026.
ocd-bill/897c73d6-df17-4716-9742-f18ad0d.comparison: Unlike CO HB 25-1311 and LA HB 639, which change operator-level taxes on net sports betting proceeds or online wagering, Iowa SSB 1152 targets only patron-level income tax withholding and leaves operators' gaming tax untouched. It is also far narrower than the framework bills in GA HB 686, HI HB 1308 and HI HB 2570, which authorize, license and tax sports wagering wholesale. Its distinguishing feature is that it ties the state withholding trigger to federal rules rather than setting a fixed dollar threshold, as Iowa does for slots, lottery and pari-mutuel winnings.
ocd-bill/897c73d6-df17-4716-9742-f18ad0d.watch: Operators should prepare payment and withholding systems so that, from January 1, 2026, Iowa withholding fires automatically on every sports wagering payout that triggers federal withholding (including after any future federal threshold changes), with remittance to the Department of Revenue handled as for slot winnings.

ocd-bill/98ce715b-357b-4f94-bd1c-a0c64cb.summary: Iowa HSB 91, a Department of Revenue proposal later renumbered HF 794, amends Iowa Code section 99F.18 to declare that all winnings from sports wagering authorized under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax. It also amends section 422.16(2)(d) to require Iowa income tax withholding on sports wagering winnings whenever federal withholding is required on the same winnings under the Internal Revenue Code. The Act takes effect January 1, 2026.
mechanics: Sec. 1 adds new subsection 2 to section 99F.18 (Tax on winnings). All winnings from chapter 99F sports wagering are Iowa earned income, and amounts deducted for state tax under section 422.16(2) must be remitted to the Department of Revenue on the winner's behalf.

Sec. 2 amends section 422.16(2)(d) to tie the state withholding trigger for sports wagering to the federal trigger: withhold state tax whenever federal income tax withholding is required on the same winnings under the IRC.
Covered parties are sports wagering licensees and operators under chapter 99F that pay out winnings subject to federal withholding.
Sec. 3 sets the effective date as January 1, 2026.
ocd-bill/98ce715b-357b-4f94-bd1c-a0c64cb.comparison: Unlike CO HB 25-1311 and LA HB 639, which change operator-level taxes, HSB 91 targets bettor income tax withholding. CO HB 25-1311 changes deductions from net sports betting proceeds, and LA HB 639 changes online sports wagering tax rates and dedications. HSB 91 leaves the operator tax untouched and instead imposes a payout-side compliance duty on operators. Also unlike GA HB 686 and HI HB 2570/HB 1308, which would create new sports betting regimes with licensing and gross revenue or excise taxes, Iowa's bill is a narrow administrative fix by the revenue department within an existing legal market. Its most unusual feature is that it sets no fixed dollar threshold for state withholding and instead conforms automatically to the federal withholding trigger.
ocd-bill/98ce715b-357b-4f94-bd1c-a0c64cb.watch: Operators should map their payout and withholding systems to the federal IRC withholding rules before January 1, 2026, since the bill sets no fixed dollar threshold. Any future federal change to sports wagering withholding (for example, the trigger amount or the 300-to-1 odds test) would automatically change Iowa withholding obligations.

ocd-bill/7cb76067-9c34-41d7-8669-66fc3cf.summary: HB 2570 HD1 (the "Representative Daniel Holt Act") adds a new HRS chapter legalizing mobile-only sports wagering in Hawaii, regulated and licensed by the Department of Business, Economic Development, and Tourism, with at least six operator licenses and a universal launch date. It taxes operators through a new privilege tax under amended HRS §237-13(9), earmarks revenue to UH Manoa athletics, a Native Hawaiian organization, an AFL-CIO affiliate, the general fund, problem gambling, and education, and creates escalating criminal penalties for unlicensed wagering. It also expressly exempts licensed sports wagering and defined fantasy sports contests from the gambling offenses in HRS ch. 712 part III.
mechanics: Licensing (§-5, §-6): DBEDT must issue a minimum of six sports wagering operator licenses, open only to a "qualified gaming entity"; $500,000 initial/renewal fee plus cost-based processing fees; five-year term; temporary licenses valid up to three years on payment of the initial fee; universal start date no later than 180 days after the Act's effective date, with equal launch for entities applying within 30 days of the application window. Supplier licenses cost $10,000 for five years, and DBEDT may accept approvals from other jurisdictions with similar standards.

Scope and wagers (§-1, §-10): mobile or digital platform only, with no kiosks or terminals at physical locations; bettors must be 21 or older and physically in Hawaii unless an interstate or international agreement under §-9 applies. Pro, collegiate, amateur, Olympic, motorsports and e-sports are covered. Youth events are excluded, as are games involving Hawaii-based colleges, including those teams' individual games within tournaments. Layoff wagers are permitted, and accounts may be funded by card, bank transfer, online payment systems, or bonuses and promotions.

Tax (§-12, §237-13(9)): operators pay the §237-13(9) privilege tax on adjusted gross sports wagering receipts using accrual accounting, in lieu of all other taxes on sports wagering. Adjusted gross receipts are gross receipts less winnings and applicable taxes, including federal excise tax, with no promotional deduction. The rate text in §237-13(9) is not in the excerpt provided. §-12(a) allocates 2% to UH Manoa athletics, 2% to a Native Hawaiian organization, 1% to the Hawaii Employees Lifeline Program (an AFL-CIO affiliate) and 10% to the general fund. §-12(b) separately directs 7% of all taxes to a new DOH problem gambling special fund (§-13) and 7% to education.

Mandatory rulemaking (§-2(f)) covers: geolocation, age and identity verification; integrity and AML; data privacy and cybersecurity; a statewide voluntary exclusion program; patron-set limits on wagers, deposits and time; and advertising rules barring targeting of minors and self-excluded persons. Rules must also prohibit bets on injuries, penalties, player discipline rulings, replay reviews and any other bet type harmful to an athlete or patron. Rules are to be consistent with other jurisdictions where commercially reasonable.

Operator duties (§-7, §-8, §-11): operators need department-approved house rules. They must run suspicious-activity monitoring software, report suspicious betting above an operator-set, department-approved threshold, and display 1-800-GAMBLER in all advertising. They must keep daily records of gross and adjusted gross receipts and honor the exclusion list, which is distributed at least quarterly.

Enforcement (§-4, §-14, §-15): civil fines of up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per occurrence, applicable to non-licensees. Unlicensed sports wagering is a misdemeanor with a minimum $10,000 fine for a first offense, a class C felony with a minimum $50,000 fine for a second, and a class B felony with a minimum $100,000 fine for a third or later. Control persons for background checks are 15% owners with control, parents and subsidiaries, and key decision-makers.
ocd-bill/7cb76067-9c34-41d7-8669-66fc3cf.comparison: Like GA HB 686, this is a full legalization-and-tax framework, but Hawaii is mobile-only, bans retail kiosks entirely and sets a floor of six licenses rather than a cap. Unlike KS SB 356, which only authorizes regulations for an existing Kansas market, or CO SB 131, which imposes specific statutory deposit caps, Hawaii leaves responsible-gaming limits and bans on certain prop and bet types to DBEDT rulemaking. On tax base, Hawaii's adjusted gross receipts deduct only winnings and taxes, with no promotional-credit deduction, which goes further than the deduction narrowing at issue in CO HB 25-1311. Its escalating felony penalties for unlicensed operators parallel AR HB 1861's approach.
ocd-bill/7cb76067-9c34-41d7-8669-66fc3cf.watch: Watch the actual §237-13(9) rate, which is absent from this excerpt, and the internally inconsistent revenue allocations in §-12(a) and (b), along with the undefined "qualified gaming entity" eligibility standard and the rule-delegated bans on injury, penalty and replay bets that could narrow the prop menu as the bill moves through JHA and CPC.

ocd-bill/98f07108-0fbd-40ae-994e-980d582.summary: HSB 330 (renumbered HF 1041) rewrites how Iowa spends money in the sports wagering receipts fund (Code 8.57I), which is fed by the sports wagering net receipts tax (99F.11(5)) and the internet fantasy sports contest tax (99E.6). Starting FY 2025-26 it sets a standing priority list of appropriations. It also makes three $10 million one-time FY 2024-25 appropriations from the fund. It does not change tax rates, licensing or any operator obligations.
mechanics: Sec. 2 replaces 8.57I(4)-(5) for FY 2025-26 onward with an ordered list paid from each year's deposits: first $1.75M to HHS for behavioral health and problem gambling prevention, treatment and recovery; next $750,000 to the Economic Development Authority, split equally among regional sports authority districts (15E.321); next $1.5M to the Department of Revenue's length of service award program grant fund (100B.52).

Under Sec. 2, the remainder is split 50% to the public safety equipment fund (80.48) and 50% to a new local emergency services equipment grant account run by the Department of Management. Eligible grantees are the 88 least populous counties and small cities as defined in 15.352, and DOM must adopt rules under chapter 17A.
Under Sec. 6, the $1.5M length of service award program allocation takes effect only if HF 1002 or SF 627 (or successor legislation) is enacted.

Sec. 4 appropriates from the fund for FY 2024-25: $10M to the community attraction and tourism fund, $10M to the Destination Iowa fund and $10M to the levee improvement fund. Sec. 5 makes this effective on enactment.

According to the explanation, Secs. 1 and 3 strike three things: the authority to use fund moneys for cash flow, the project reporting requirements, and the requirement that county endowment grantees consider racetrack-operating charities when using sports wagering money (no such transfers occur under current law).
ocd-bill/98f07108-0fbd-40ae-994e-980d582.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. What is unusual is that the bill deals only with where existing sports wagering and fantasy sports tax revenue goes, not with the rate or base. It also earmarks most of the residual revenue for public safety and rural emergency equipment rather than the general fund or education.
ocd-bill/98f07108-0fbd-40ae-994e-980d582.watch: The bill leaves rates untouched, but operators should watch HF 1041 for amendments, because tying sports wagering receipts to public safety and rural emergency grants creates constituencies that may later push for higher net receipts tax rates or a broader tax base to grow the 50/50 residual pool.

ocd-bill/9f858c80-81ac-4d57-a1b1-ce7c7f7.summary: Idaho H 133 (Session Law Chapter 64, effective July 1, 2025) rewrites the Clean Indoor Air Act and the Prevention of Minors' Access to Tobacco statute. It adds and revises definitions, replaces the old rulemaking section with a sign-posting standard, and adds permit endorsements for delivery and direct sales. It also adjusts the civil penalty and inspection provisions and voids IDAPA 16.07.25 and 16.02.23. Its only gambling content is a cross-reference correction in Section 12 to Idaho Code 56-227F, which already bars using TAFI benefit cards for gambling, pari-mutuel betting or lottery purchases and requires licensed gambling establishments to comply.
mechanics: Section 1 amends 39-5502 to add definitions including 'educational facility,' 'enclosed,' 'person in charge' and 'tobacco products.' It extends smoke-free zones to within 20 feet of entrances to hospitals, arenas, terminals and schools.

Section 3 creates a new 39-5508 requiring no-smoking signs with letters at least 1 inch high. Sections 4-5 define 'location' (including the URL of internet-only retailers) and 'permit endorsement' (delivery sales, delivery service, direct sales); applicants must select one or more endorsements on annually renewed permits.

Section 7 (39-5708) sets the penalty ladder: a non-permittee seller is fined $100; a second violation brings a $200 fine, waived if a training program and signed employee form are on file; a third violation in two years brings $200 ($400 for a repeat employee) and up to a 7-day suspension; four or more violations bring $400 and revocation of at least 30 days. Fines are due within 10 days.
Section 8 (39-5710) requires at least one random, unannounced inspection per year at every retail location, with minor-assisted checks except for minor-exempt permittees.

Section 12 updates a code citation in 56-227F, which bars TAFI EBT use for gaming under chapters 38 and 49 of title 18, tribal-compact gaming, pari-mutuel betting and the lottery; licensed gambling establishments must block EBT use or risk having their BIN and ATM access disabled.
Sections 13-14 void IDAPA 16.07.25 and 16.02.23 as of July 1, 2025.
ocd-bill/9f858c80-81ac-4d57-a1b1-ce7c7f7.comparison: Unlike the sports wagering frameworks in HI HB 1308 and HB 2570, the betting-protection and regulatory bills in CO SB 131 and SB 163, the fantasy contest bill KY HB 904, and the sweepstakes measure CA AB 831, this is a tobacco and vaping bill with no substantive gaming provisions. Its only gaming touchpoint is a technical citation fix to Idaho's existing ban on using public assistance cards at gambling establishments, which the bill leaves unchanged. The closest analog is IA SSB 3199, an omnibus bill that also touches nicotine and vapor products, but it is a broader budget vehicle.
ocd-bill/9f858c80-81ac-4d57-a1b1-ce7c7f7.watch: Nothing new for sports-betting operators: the only gaming-related text is an unchanged EBT and gambling-establishment restriction in 56-227F, which is relevant only to the extent an operator holds an Idaho gambling license or runs ATMs on premises.

ocd-bill/9de421df-a6dc-4ff9-805b-7f83729.summary: HB 2592 is an omnibus tax-base broadening bill that repeals selected Arizona tax exemptions. For gaming, Section 1 amends A.R.S. 5-111(C) so that the state's pari-mutuel percentage, which previously did not apply to wagering on simulcasts of out-of-state races, now also applies to those pools. The rest of the visible text repeals transaction privilege tax retail exemptions for warranty and service contracts and for sales of stocks and bonds, with conforming renumbering across Titles 28 and 42.
mechanics: Sec. 1, A.R.S. 5-111(C): the state's take of 2% of the first $1,000,000 of daily pari-mutuel pools and 5% of the amount above $1,000,000 is extended to pools on simulcasts of out-of-state races, repealing the existing carve-out.

The existing 5-111 exemptions are retained in the shown text: county fair racing meetings (D), charity racing days (E), unclaimed tickets from unclaimed property law (F), and permittee pari-mutuel receipts and purse monies from Title 42, Chapter 5 TPT (G).

Sec. 5, A.R.S. 42-5061(A): repeals the retail TPT exclusions for sales of warranty or service contracts (former para. 3) and for the sale of stocks and bonds (former para. 7), and renumbers the remaining paragraphs.
Secs. 2-4 (28-2154.01, 42-5008.01, 42-5009) make conforming cross-reference changes to reflect the renumbering.
The title also lists amendments to 42-5071, 42-5072, 42-5075, 42-6017 and 43-1111, but those sections fall outside the supplied text, which is truncated at 42-5061(A)(34).
No effective date or enforcement provision appears in the supplied text. Status: second reading in the House on 2025-01-28.
ocd-bill/9de421df-a6dc-4ff9-805b-7f83729.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639 (online sports wagering tax changes) and CO HB 25-1311 (limits on operator deductions from net sports betting proceeds), HB 2592 does not touch Arizona's event wagering tax. Its gaming hook is narrower: removing a pari-mutuel simulcast exemption for horse racing. It also differs from the IA withholding bills (SF 605, SSB 1152, HSB 91), which target bettor winnings rather than operator or permittee liability. What is unusual is that a gaming tax increase is folded into a general exemption-repeal bill instead of a standalone gaming measure.
ocd-bill/9de421df-a6dc-4ff9-805b-7f83729.watch: Watch whether this exemption-repeal approach widens in amendment to reach event wagering deductions or other Title 5 carve-outs, and how much extending the state's 2% to 5% take to out-of-state simulcast pools would raise costs for racetrack permittees and the advance-deposit or simulcast wagering clients.

ocd-bill/a3b46953-12c5-42c1-9a1f-aba2ce8.summary: Act 491 amends R.S. 27:27.2 to require the Louisiana Gaming Control Board to adopt rules creating a separate exclusion list for retail sports books and mobile wagering, covering people already on the general gaming exclusion list, people who threaten violence or harm against anyone involved in a sporting event where the threat relates to sports gaming, and anyone the board finds threatens the state's interests or effective sports wagering regulation. It makes clear that both the board and the division can place people on exclusion lists, bars listing based on race, color, creed, national origin, sex or disability, and re-letters the existing notice, petition, penalty, sanction and hearing provisions. Effective August 1, 2026.
mechanics: New R.S. 27:27.2(B): the board must adopt rules for a list of persons to be excluded or ejected from retail sports books and barred from the play or operation of mobile wagering under a license or contract issued under Title 27.

Three listing categories under (B): (1) persons excluded under Subsection A; (2) persons who, before, during or after a sporting event, threaten violence or harm against any person involved in the event, where the threat is related to sports gaming; (3) persons the board determines pose a threat to the state's interests, the purposes of Title 27, or the strict and effective regulation of sports wagering.
New (C): the board and the division may both place persons on the list, but not because of race, color, creed, national origin, sex or disability (as defined in R.S. 51:2232).

Carried-over provisions, re-lettered: notice by personal service or certified mail (D); a petition for removal, where the petitioner bears the burden of proof (E); entering or attempting to enter after listing is punishable by up to 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to $500 (F); and a hearing within 30 days of the petition under R.S. 27:25 (H).

Operator exposure under (G): the board may sanction licensees, permittees or the casino operator for willful failure to exclude a listed person, and may seek suspension or revocation for a pattern of willful failure.
Effective August 1, 2026, as Act No. 491. Video draw poker licensees remain exempt under (I).
ocd-bill/a3b46953-12c5-42c1-9a1f-aba2ce8.comparison: No comparable bills from other states were listed. The unusual feature is that it ties exclusion from sports wagering, including mobile accounts, to threats of violence against athletes, officials or others involved in a sporting event when the threat is linked to betting. That targets bettor harassment rather than the traditional casino exclusion grounds such as cheating or criminal history. The catch-all in (B)(3) gives the board broad discretion to exclude anyone it deems a threat to effective sports wagering regulation.
ocd-bill/a3b46953-12c5-42c1-9a1f-aba2ce8.watch: Watch the board's implementing rules for how mobile operators must identify, block and eject listed persons, and how 'willful failure to exclude' under Section 27.2(G) will be applied to online accounts, because that failure is a basis for sanctions and, if it forms a pattern, license suspension or revocation.

ocd-bill/a542e540-0501-4f86-ad7f-52e8d94.summary: Act 810 rewrites Louisiana's college NIL statute (R.S. 17:3701 et seq.) and, in new R.S. 17:3705, extends NIL rights to high school athletes for the first time. The high school provisions ban NIL compensation tied to a list of restricted categories that includes gaming, gambling, or wagering, expressly including sports wagering. The college provisions update agent rules, raise disclosure obligations to a $600 threshold, broaden institutional liability shields, and require management-board NIL policies.
mechanics: New R.S. 17:3705(E)(2)(d) bars interscholastic athletes (students in grades 9-12 at public or nonpublic high schools) from earning NIL compensation in connection with "gaming, gambling, or wagering, including but not limited to sports wagering." The same list covers alcohol, cannabis, adult entertainment, tobacco and vapor products, weapons, and performance-enhancing drugs.

Under 3705(B), NIL agreements signed by high school athletes under 18 are valid only with written parental or guardian consent. Under 3705(G), athletes must disclose proposed agreements to the school before signing, and under 3705(J) an aggrieved athlete may sue for injunctive relief.

High schools and athletic associations may not bar NIL earnings or representation, or declare an athlete ineligible for engaging in them (3705(C)-(D)). Schools may still restrict NIL activity during team or academic activities, block deals that conflict with existing school agreements, and control use of school marks (3705(F)).
Under R.S. 17:3703(I), college athletes must disclose NIL contracts worth $600 or more to their institution, with reporting rules aligned to the applicable athletic governing commission.

R.S. 17:3703(D) requires athlete agents to be registered under R.S. 4:422 and comply with the federal SPARTA. Section 3703(L) shields institutions, affiliated nonprofits, and staff from liability over third-party NIL deals, except for gross negligence or intentional misconduct.

Section 3703(N) requires management boards to adopt NIL policies covering compensation, institutional involvement, use of marks, representation, education, enforcement, and a compliance contact. Institutions cannot implement the Chapter until their board acts.
ocd-bill/a542e540-0501-4f86-ad7f-52e8d94.comparison: Like HI HB 2384 and KY SB 3, LA HB 513 adapts state NIL law to the post-settlement institutional-agreement era, with board-adopted policies and disclosure requirements. Unlike either of those, it extends NIL rights to high school athletes and expressly bars minors' NIL deals involving sports wagering. KY HB 904 is a gaming-regulation bill on fantasy contests and is not comparable in substance. The only overlap is that both touch on who may be marketed to or associated with wagering products.
ocd-bill/a542e540-0501-4f86-ad7f-52e8d94.watch: Operators and their marketing affiliates should screen influencer and endorsement programs to exclude Louisiana high school athletes under R.S. 17:3705(E)(2)(d). Note that this Act imposes no comparable gaming ban on college athletes, so any restrictions there come from LGCB advertising rules and institutional policies.

ocd-bill/a84ca18c-662b-4c51-9b5c-7b6887e.summary: HB 2384 HD2 adds a new subpart to HRS chapter 304A creating a name, image, and likeness (NIL) framework for University of Hawaii student-athletes. It affirms their right to earn NIL compensation, requires the university to adopt NIL, disclosure, agent, education, and Title IX policies, and requires annual aggregate reporting to the legislature. Its only gaming link is that the university may bar student-athletes from NIL deals involving gambling or sports wagering.
mechanics: New §304A-(c)(3) lets the university prohibit NIL agreements involving "gambling, sports wagering, or illegal drugs," alongside adult entertainment, firearms, tobacco/vaping, and any industry that conflicts with the university's mission or financial interests.

Student-athletes must disclose third-party NIL deals worth $600 or more, or an alternative threshold set by NCAA rules or federal law. They may rescind any institutional or third-party NIL agreement within at least ten business days of signing.

The university, conferences, and the NCAA may not unduly restrict NIL activity, except to comply with law, post-House settlement governing-body rules, or reasonable, neutral policies on conflicts of interest, time commitments, or prohibited industries.

Annual reports to the legislature begin with the 2028 session and cover state-funded institutional NIL spending by team and gender, compliance measures, and violations. Underlying records are exempt from chapter 92F disclosure.
Section 3 makes a general-fund appropriation for FY2026-27, with the amount left blank, including for direct institutional NIL payments.
Section 5 sets a placeholder effective date of July 1, 3000, a sunset of June 30, 2030, and a planned legislative review in the 2029 session.
ocd-bill/a84ca18c-662b-4c51-9b5c-7b6887e.comparison: Like KY SB 3 and LA HB 513, this is a student-athlete NIL bill updating state law after the House v. NCAA settlement. Hawaii's version is limited to the University of Hawaii, whereas LA HB 513 also reaches interscholastic athletes. Unlike KY HB 904, which directly regulates gaming (fantasy contest operators, geolocation), HB 2384 touches wagering only through a permissive prohibited-industries list for NIL endorsements. Its defective 3000 effective date and blank appropriation signal it is still a vehicle for conference negotiation.
ocd-bill/a84ca18c-662b-4c51-9b5c-7b6887e.watch: Watch whether the permissive gambling and sports-wagering NIL exclusion in §304A-(c)(3) is hardened into a mandatory ban, or broadened, as the bill moves through EDU and WAM/CPN, since that would limit operator sponsorship and endorsement deals with UH athletes if Hawaii ever authorizes wagering.

ocd-bill/afab5429-2e04-4b6a-b154-8b41412.summary: SB 1735 is Arizona's FY2025-26 general appropriations act. It amends Laws 2024, ch. 209 to adjust FY2024-25 appropriations for the Department of Child Safety (§25) and the Department of Corrections (§31), and it cuts a state highway fund transfer (§134). It then makes line-item FY2025-26 appropriations to state agencies. The excerpt provided contains no provisions on sports betting, wagering, or gaming regulation.
mechanics: Sec. 1 raises the DCS FY2024-25 total from $1,262,616,900 to $1,322,004,400, with increases to caseworkers, congregate care and comprehensive health plan services.
Sec. 2 lowers the Department of Corrections FY2024-25 total from $1,584,593,700 to $1,566,154,400, mainly by cutting noncontract medication from $55M to $18M.
Sec. 3 reduces the FY2024-25 state highway fund transfer to the general fund from $18.7M to $17.2M.
Sec. 4 limits each appropriation to its listed fund source; if that source is unavailable, no other source may be used.
Secs. 5-13 make FY2025-26 appropriations, including AHCCCS at about $22.0B, Department of Administration at $296.8M and Attorney General at $98.5M, with JLBC review and reporting conditions.
ocd-bill/afab5429-2e04-4b6a-b154-8b41412.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. The provided text stops partway through the Attorney General section (Sec. 13) and never reaches any Department of Gaming or event wagering line item. Nothing in the excerpt touches wagering tax rates, licensing, advertising or integrity rules. Any gaming relevance would come from portions of the act not reproduced here.
ocd-bill/afab5429-2e04-4b6a-b154-8b41412.watch: Check the full enacted act (not in this excerpt) for the Department of Gaming appropriation and any fund transfers or sweeps from gaming-related funds that could affect regulatory staffing or fee-funded operations.

ocd-bill/a87e6074-85dc-4669-ba85-8857b76.summary: SSB 3199 is Iowa's omnibus standings and appropriations bill for FY 2026-27, covering appropriation limits, fund transfers, corrective amendments and unrelated policy items such as the national electrical code, local civil rights ordinances and noxious weeds. Its gaming content is limited to two fiscal provisions: a new permanent $1 million annual draw on the sports wagering receipts fund, and authority to pay state salary adjustments from the gaming enforcement and gaming regulatory revolving funds. The text provided is cut off around page 18 of 41, so later divisions (tax credits, alternative nicotine and vapor products and others named in the title) were not reviewed.
mechanics: Sec. 7 adds Iowa Code 8.57I(3)(c): starting FY 2026-27 and every year after, $1,000,000 is appropriated from the sports wagering receipts fund to HHS for a grant to the Iowa Healthiest State Initiative's Double Up Food Bucks program, which helps SNAP recipients buy fresh produce.
The grantee must provide at least a dollar-for-dollar match, and 8.57I subsections 5 and 6 are made inapplicable to this money.

Sec. 6 lets the Department of Management fund FY 2026-27 salary adjustments from unappropriated money in the gaming enforcement and gaming regulatory revolving funds, alongside other special funds, subject to constitutional limits.

Non-gaming items include $100.5M+ in HHS IT appropriations from the information technology fund (Sec. 5), a $32.5M annual cut to area education agency special education state aid (Sec. 10), and an Iowa-specific 2023 National Electrical Code with local preemption (Secs. 35-37).
Effective dates vary by provision; Sec. 7 operates from July 1, 2026.
ocd-bill/a87e6074-85dc-4669-ba85-8857b76.comparison: Like KS HB 2513 and CO SB 25-107, this is a general appropriations vehicle and does not alter sports wagering licensing, tax rates or conduct rules. It is closest to LA HB 639, which also dedicates gaming revenue. LA HB 639 pairs that dedication with changes to the online sports wagering tax, whereas SSB 3199 only reallocates money already collected in Iowa's sports wagering receipts fund, adding a permanent $1M carve-out for a nutrition program. Unlike HI HB 2570, HI HB 1308 or GA HB 686, it creates no regulatory framework.
ocd-bill/a87e6074-85dc-4669-ba85-8857b76.watch: Watch whether the permanent $1M sports wagering receipts carve-out and the use of gaming regulatory and enforcement revolving funds for salary adjustments signal a broader legislative appetite to tap wagering revenue or raise regulatory fees, and review the untruncated remainder of the bill for any other gaming references.

ocd-bill/ab4674de-7162-456c-a34f-b3a4417.summary: HB 1861 amends Arkansas's keeping-a-gambling-house offense (§ 5-66-103) to cover online gambling. It expressly reaches dual-currency sweepstakes that simulate casino games, lottery games, or sports wagering and award cash or cash equivalents, and any online game that regulators define by rule as sports wagering. It also creates an Interactive Gaming Act (new §§ 23-117-201 to -208) letting the state's Amendment 100 casino licensees offer online casino gaming and a novel name, image, or likeness (NIL) drawing game under Arkansas Racing Commission approval, and makes unlicensed operation of an interactive gaming system a Class D felony. The bill was recommended for interim study on April 7, 2025, so it is effectively stalled for the 2025 session.
mechanics: Section 1 adds § 5-66-103(a)(4): offering an internet or mobile game that uses a dual-currency system redeemable for cash, cash equivalents, or prizes, and that simulates casino games, lottery games, or sports wagering, is keeping a gambling house. Sweepstakes that do not award cash or cash equivalents are carved out, as are commission-licensed casinos.

Section 1 adds § 5-66-103(a)(5): operating any online game that the Racing Commission or the Department of Finance and Administration determines by rule to be sports wagering is also covered. Licensed casinos and the Scholarship Lottery are excluded.

Online casino structure (§ 23-117-203): only Amendment 100 casino licensees may offer interactive gaming, using a commission-approved system. Each licensee is limited to one branded system. Interactive gaming is prohibited if a majority of net casino gaming receipts from it is paid to a third-party vendor.

Technical and operating rules: systems must meet GLI-19 (July 17, 2020 revision) or an equivalent commission-approved certification, and core servers must be hosted in the United States with play confined to Arkansas. The commission approves game titles and themes. Live dealers must be licensed where they physically work, and licensees must report them to the commission at least monthly.

NIL drawing game (§§ 23-117-202(5), -203(c)): a commission-approved drawing game whose net proceeds are split between an NIL collective or other organization affiliated with an Arkansas collegiate athletics program and the winner. The emergency clause describes the split as equal.

Dormant accounts and enforcement: an account is dormant after 16 months without patron activity and may be suspended, with ID re-verification required to reactivate. Funds left 2 years after dormancy go to a commission cash fund, and the licensee must try to contact the holder at least once a year. Unlicensed operation of an interactive gaming system is a Class D felony (§ 23-117-207). An emergency clause makes the act effective on enactment.
ocd-bill/ab4674de-7162-456c-a34f-b3a4417.comparison: Like CA AB 831, HB 1861 targets dual-currency sweepstakes that simulate casino games, but it does so through Arkansas's criminal gambling-house statute and also explicitly covers simulated lottery and sports wagering. By contrast, GA HB 686 and HI HB 2570/HB 1308 build standalone sports wagering licensing and tax regimes, whereas HB 1861 sets no tax rate or license fee and folds iGaming into existing Amendment 100 casino licenses under Racing Commission rulemaking. Its NIL drawing game, which routes gaming proceeds to collegiate NIL collectives, has no analogue in the listed bills, including KY SB 3's NIL changes and KY HB 904's fantasy contest regulation.
ocd-bill/ab4674de-7162-456c-a34f-b3a4417.watch: Watch the § 5-66-103(a)(5) delegation letting the Racing Commission or DFA define "sports wagering" by rule, which could pull DFS, pick'em, or other contest products into felony gambling-house exposure, along with the one-skin-per-casino limit and the bar on paying a vendor a majority of iGaming receipts, which together restrict how national operators can partner with Arkansas casinos if the bill returns.

ocd-bill/b009758a-d932-4ce5-acfd-31595b9.summary: HB 1308 HD3 SD2 would legalize mobile-only sports wagering in Hawaii through a new HRS chapter administered by the Department of Law Enforcement, which must issue at least four operator licenses to qualified gaming entities and set a universal start date no later than 180 days after the effective date. Operators would pay a 10% tax on adjusted gross sports wagering receipts, imposed through a new general excise tax paragraph, HRS 237-13(9). The bill also sets up a voluntary exclusion program and a problem gambling special fund, and creates escalating criminal penalties for unlicensed sports wagering.
mechanics: Licensing: at least four operator licenses at $250,000 (initial or renewal), plus a supplier license at $10,000, each with cost-based processing fees and a five-year term. Temporary licenses of up to three years are available if the full fee is paid with the application. Only a 'qualified gaming entity' may apply, meaning one that offers online sports wagering in the State or in at least three U.S. jurisdictions under a state regulatory structure (sections -5 and -6).

Tax: 10% of adjusted gross receipts, defined as gross receipts minus winnings actually paid. There is no express deduction for promotional or free-bet credits. The tax uses accrual accounting and is 'in lieu of all other taxes' on sports wagering. Of collections, 7% goes to a DOH problem gambling special fund and 7% to education programs (section -11 and new HRS 237-13(9)).

Scope: wagering is mobile or digital only, with no kiosks or terminals at physical locations. Bettors must be 21 or older and located in-state unless an interstate or international agreement under section -9 applies. Collegiate, amateur, Olympic, motorsport and esports events are allowed; youth events are barred. Props, parlays, in-play and exchange wagering are expressly included, and fantasy contests are excluded.

Operator duties (section -8): integrity monitoring software for unusual volume or odds swings, with prompt reporting to the department; reporting of suspicious betting above an operator-set, department-approved threshold; department approval of house rules; daily receipts records; and display of 1-800-GAMBLER in all advertising. Layoff wagers between operators are allowed with disclosure, and operators must allow patrons to fund accounts with bonuses or promotions.

Applicant vetting: control persons (holders of 15% or more with control, parent and subsidiary companies, and key decision-makers) must undergo FBI fingerprint checks, unless they were checked within the prior 12 months. Material changes must be reported within 30 days. Grounds for denial or revocation include a gambling license revoked by another regulator and lack of financial responsibility.

Enforcement: violations of the chapter are civil, with fines up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per occurrence, and fines may be imposed on non-licensees. Unlicensed sports wagering is a misdemeanor with a fine of at least $10,000 for a first offense, a class C felony with at least $50,000 for a second, and a class B felony with at least $100,000 for a third or later offense.
ocd-bill/b009758a-d932-4ce5-acfd-31595b9.comparison: Like GA HB 686, this is a full legalization and licensing bill, but Hawaii's version is mobile-only with no retail or tribal tether, has a license floor rather than a cap, and has a relatively low 10% rate. That contrasts with the rate increase on online wagering in LA HB 639. Its definition of adjusted gross receipts deducts only winnings paid, which raises the same promotional-deduction question Colorado is legislating in CO HB 25-1311. Its consumer protections are thinner than CO SB 131's deposit limits, being limited to voluntary exclusion and a helpline notice. Its graduated felony penalties for unlicensed operation parallel the approach in AR HB 1861.
ocd-bill/b009758a-d932-4ce5-acfd-31595b9.watch: Watch the conference committee outcome on the tax rate, the base, and the minimum number of licenses, because the current text does not expressly allow deduction of promotional credits even though operators must accept bonuses as a funding method. Also watch new HRS 237-13(9), which as drafted would apply the 10% AGR tax to 'sports wagering suppliers' as well as operators.

ocd-bill/b16e19f4-4200-4f40-aee7-093a0ce.summary: Colorado SB 163 is a regulatory clean-up and enforcement bill for the Limited Gaming Act of 1991 and sports betting law. It lets the Limited Gaming Control Commission delegate more licensing duties to the Division of Gaming, authorizes division investigators to inspect and impound premises suspected of unlicensed gaming or sports betting, and extends the voluntary self-exclusion program to sports betting. It also moves game pre-approval from the commission to the division and clarifies the fingerprint-based background check process.
mechanics: The commission may delegate to the Division of Gaming licensing duties found anywhere in the gaming act, not only the specific duties currently listed.
Division investigators and their supervisors may inspect, examine, investigate, hold, or impound any premises in Colorado where they suspect unlicensed gaming or unlicensed sports betting.
The division's voluntary self-exclusion program, which currently covers gaming, is expanded to cover sports betting.
A designee of the director is a peace officer while performing their duties, with primary authority that includes enforcing all state laws.
Licensees need prior approval from the division, rather than the commission, before offering certain games.

The bill clarifies the definition of 'race meet', adds other gaming definitions, and clarifies how the commission and the Colorado Bureau of Investigation run fingerprint-based background checks on license applicants. Full text was unavailable, so the specific statutory sections and effective date could not be confirmed.
ocd-bill/b16e19f4-4200-4f40-aee7-093a0ce.comparison: Unlike the authorization and tax bills on the list (GA HB 686, HI HB 2570 and HB 1308, LA HB 639, IA SF 613 and SSB 1157), CO SB 163 does not touch tax rates or market structure; it is administrative and enforcement housekeeping for an existing market. Its enforcement against unlicensed operators parallels AR HB 1861, which makes operating an illegal online casino or sportsbook a felony, though Colorado uses administrative inspection and impoundment rather than new criminal penalties. Its shift of authority from commission to agency resembles Kentucky's HB 566 corporation clean-up and Kansas SB 356's grant of rulemaking authority to the racing and gaming commission.
ocd-bill/b16e19f4-4200-4f40-aee7-093a0ce.watch: Operators should watch for division rulemaking that sets up the sports-betting self-exclusion program, including how exclusion lists are shared with operators, compliance obligations, and liability for serving excluded patrons, along with any faster or stricter game-approval process now that the division, not the commission, grants approval.

ocd-bill/b542eca5-6011-4308-a6a3-d5b83f8.summary: HB 379 amends Alabama's Entertainment Industry Incentive Act of 2009 to add a small-production rebate of 45 percent of Alabama-resident payroll for productions spending $100,000 to $499,999, funded from an annual reserve of up to $2 million. It also tightens when payments to loan-out companies count toward the rebate, lowers the spending thresholds for soundtrack and music video projects, and pushes the out-of-state program evaluation report to the 2028 Regular Session. Its only connection to gaming is a pre-existing exclusion of gambling, wagering and pari-mutuel activity from the definition of a qualified production.
mechanics: New §41-7A-43(b): the office may reserve up to $2,000,000 a year for small-budget productions, which earn a rebate of 45% of Alabama-resident payroll if total production expenditures are $100,000 to $499,999.
The main rebate is unchanged at 25% of non-resident-payroll expenditures plus 35% of resident payroll, with a $500,000 minimum and no rebate on spending above the first $20,000,000.

Under §41-7A-42(6) and (7)d, loan-out company payments count toward the rebate only if the production company withholds and remits Alabama tax at the highest rate under §40-18-71 or §40-18-5/§40-18-31. A loan-out company's failure to file its return does not disqualify the payments.
Soundtrack and music video minimums drop from $50,000 to $30,000, and the soundtrack cap drops from $300,000 to $200,000.
§41-7A-42(8)b keeps the exclusion of any form of gambling, gaming, wagering, or pari-mutuel wagering activity or enterprise from 'qualified production'; sporting events productions are also excluded.
The evaluation report deadline moves to the 1st legislative day of the 2028 session; the program sunset stays at December 31, 2028; the act takes effect October 1, 2026.
ocd-bill/b542eca5-6011-4308-a6a3-d5b83f8.comparison: No comparable bills from other states were listed. The bill is a film and entertainment tax-incentive measure. Its only gaming touchpoint is existing language barring gambling, wagering and pari-mutuel enterprises, and sporting-event productions, from incentive eligibility, which the bill carries forward unchanged.
ocd-bill/b542eca5-6011-4308-a6a3-d5b83f8.watch: Operators should note that the retained §41-7A-42(8)b exclusion keeps gambling-related and sporting-event content, such as betting shows or wagering-integrated digital media, ineligible for Alabama's entertainment rebates, though the bill otherwise has no effect on gaming.

ocd-bill/b51878cd-644f-46b3-b328-c536f6f.summary: HB 25-1311 accelerates and then ends the free bets (promotional) deduction Colorado sports betting operators may take when calculating monthly net sports betting proceeds, the base for the state's sports betting tax. Under prior law the cap was 2% of total monthly bets through June 30, 2026, then 1.75% indefinitely. The act shortens the 2% period to December 31, 2025, applies 1.75% only from January 1 through June 30, 2026, and prohibits any free bets deduction from July 1, 2026.
mechanics: Amends C.R.S. 44-30-1501(7)(c)(I)(C): the free bets deduction cap of no more than 2% of total monthly bets now runs July 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025, instead of through June 30, 2026.
Amends (7)(c)(I)(D): the 1.75% cap now applies only from January 1, 2026 through June 30, 2026. Before this act, 1.75% was the permanent rate from July 1, 2026.
Adds (7)(c)(I.5): on and after July 1, 2026, neither sports betting operators nor internet sports betting operators may deduct any free bets placed by players.

Section 2 appropriates $17,135 to the Department of Revenue for FY 2025-26 from the sports betting fund (44-30-1509(1)(a)). Of that, $13,906 is for GenTax IT support, $1,024 for taxation personal services and $2,205 for executive director's office administration.

Section 3 makes the act effective 90 days after the General Assembly adjourns, which is after the July 1, 2025 start of the 2% tier. A referendum petition would delay effect until approval at the November 2026 general election.
ocd-bill/b51878cd-644f-46b3-b328-c536f6f.comparison: Unlike the comprehensive authorization bills in GA HB 686 and HI HB 2570/HB 1308, which build licensing and tax regimes from scratch, CO HB 25-1311 is a narrow tax-base change in a mature market. It raises effective tax by eliminating the promotional deduction rather than raising the rate. It is closest in subject to LA HB 639, which addresses taxation of online sports wagering, and to Iowa's tax-rate measures in SF 613 and SSB 1157, though those bills' summaries do not indicate a promotional-deduction phase-out. Iowa's SF 605, SSB 1152 and HSB 91 address withholding on player winnings, not operator taxable revenue.
ocd-bill/b51878cd-644f-46b3-b328-c536f6f.watch: Operators should model the loss of the free bets deduction on January 1, 2026 (cap cut to 1.75%) and its full elimination on July 1, 2026, revise Colorado promotional spending and tax reporting accordingly, and watch for any referendum petition that could delay the act until November 2026.

ocd-bill/c4c97b57-a75b-4448-8b8c-76028db.summary: Georgia House Resolution 1908 is a ceremonial resolution recognizing and commending Akbar Muhammad, a historian, international-affairs consultant and founder of the Youth4Africa Foundation, for his work promoting travel and business ties with Africa. It contains no provisions on sports betting, gaming, wagering or any regulatory matter. Its only operative directive is that the Clerk of the House distribute a copy to Mr. Muhammad.
mechanics: Lines 32-34: the House recognizes and commends Akbar Muhammad and extends best wishes for his health, happiness and success.
Lines 35-37: the Clerk of the House is directed to make a copy of the resolution available to Mr. Muhammad.
No statutory amendments, rates, definitions, effective dates or enforcement provisions.
Status: read and adopted by the House on 2026-03-25. As a single-chamber resolution, no further action is needed.
ocd-bill/c4c97b57-a75b-4448-8b8c-76028db.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. The resolution is a routine Georgia commendation with no gaming content. Its only connection to sports is a passing mention (lines 10-12) that Mr. Muhammad arranged Africa travel for people including 'major sports figures.'
ocd-bill/c4c97b57-a75b-4448-8b8c-76028db.watch: Nothing to watch: this is a non-binding honorary resolution with no bearing on sports-betting or gaming operators, and it can be dropped from tracking.

ocd-bill/c3da83ee-ab23-4d12-94d4-f5e6538.summary: SB 1274 is Arizona's 2025 technical tax corrections bill, signed by the Governor on May 13, 2025, amending A.R.S. 42-1008, 42-5001, 42-5061, 43-403, 43-405, 43-1014 and 43-1414 and Laws 2023, ch. 147, sec. 3. Its only gaming touchpoint in the text provided is a cross-reference fix to the transaction privilege tax retail-classification exemption for lottery tickets. It does not regulate or tax sports wagering.
mechanics: Sec. 1 (42-1008): extends the ban on preparing tax returns for compensation from Department of Revenue employees to individuals acting as DOR agents or contractors and their managers or supervisors; a violation is grounds for dismissal or removal from contracted duties.

Sec. 3 (42-5061(A)(20)): the retail TPT deduction for lottery tickets or shares now cross-references title 5, chapter 5.1, article 2 instead of article 1, a conforming correction with no apparent substantive change.
Sec. 2 (42-5001): restates the TPT definitions, with an apparent change requiring qualifying health care organizations' annual audits to be filed annually with the department.
The bill also amends income tax sections 43-403 and 43-405 (withholding), 43-1014 and 43-1414, and Laws 2023, ch. 147, sec. 3, but that text is not in the excerpt provided.
The text reviewed is the introduced version, so the enacted text may differ.
ocd-bill/c3da83ee-ab23-4d12-94d4-f5e6538.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639 (online sports wagering tax rates), CO HB 25-1311 (limits on deductions from net sports betting proceeds) or IA SF 605, SSB 1152 and HSB 91 (state withholding on sports wagering winnings), SB 1274 does not change any wagering tax rate, base or deduction. It is closer in kind to omnibus revenue cleanup bills such as KY HB 757 and FL HB 7031, where gaming appears only through a cross-reference. Its lottery reference correction is purely conforming.
ocd-bill/c3da83ee-ab23-4d12-94d4-f5e6538.watch: Pull the enacted text of the amended withholding sections, A.R.S. 43-403 and 43-405, which are not in the excerpt reviewed, to confirm nothing alters withholding or reporting on gambling or event wagering winnings, the issue Iowa's SF 605 targets.

ocd-bill/c72ca5a4-692d-4f12-a2ac-77e5f98.summary: SF 165 authorizes Iowa municipalities (cities, counties, townships, benefited fire districts, and emergency response agencies) to create IRC section 457(e)(11) length of service award programs for volunteer fire fighters, volunteer EMS providers, and reserve peace officers. It funds a new state grant fund for those programs entirely from the sports wagering receipts fund under Code section 8.57I: a $1.5 million appropriation for FY2025-26, then an annual top-up to a $1.5 million balance. The bill does not change sports wagering taxes, licensing, or conduct rules; its only gaming link is that it redirects sports wagering revenue.
mechanics: Sec. 4: appropriates $1,500,000 from the sports wagering receipts fund to the Department of Revenue for FY beginning July 1, 2025, for deposit in the new length of service award program grant fund.

Sec. 1 (new 8.57I(3A)): starting FY beginning July 1, 2026, and every year after, transfers from the sports wagering receipts fund whatever amount is needed to bring the grant fund's unencumbered balance to $1.5 million as of July 1. These transfers are exempt from the reporting requirements in 8.57I subsections 4 and 5.

Sec. 3 (new 100B.52): the grant fund sits under the Department of Revenue. Grants are up to a dollar-for-dollar match, capped at $300 per award recipient per year. Interest stays in the fund, and unspent money does not revert at year end.

Sec. 2 (new 100B.51): municipalities choosing to set up a program adopt eligibility, vesting, and distribution guidelines in consultation with fire and police chiefs. Awards must be structured as tax-deferred benefits.
Municipalities may use gifts, devises, bequests, or other sources to provide their local match. The Department of Revenue must adopt Chapter 17A rules for the grant application process.
Status: committee report approved, and the bill was renumbered as SF 627 on 2025-04-16.
ocd-bill/c72ca5a4-692d-4f12-a2ac-77e5f98.comparison: Unlike the substantive gaming bills listed, SF 165 does not regulate operators or alter tax rates or deductions. Those bills include GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570 (legalization and licensing), CO HB 25-1311 (net proceeds deductions), and CO SB 131 (deposit limits). It is closest to LA HB 639, which dedicates gaming revenues, and to appropriations vehicles like KS HB 2513, in that it earmarks existing sports wagering receipts for an unrelated public purpose. What is unusual is the open-ended, self-replenishing annual draw on the sports wagering receipts fund, paired with an exemption from that fund's normal reporting requirements.
ocd-bill/c72ca5a4-692d-4f12-a2ac-77e5f98.watch: Operators should watch whether this recurring $1.5 million top-up becomes one of a growing set of claims on Iowa's sports wagering receipts fund, which could build pressure to raise the tax rate or curtail deductions to sustain dedicated programs.

ocd-bill/c6d93f23-fe9e-458f-a524-258d706.summary: HB 757 is Kentucky's 2026 omnibus revenue bill, enacted with an emergency clause as Acts Ch. 161. It updates Kentucky's Internal Revenue Code conformity date to December 31, 2025, decouples from several new federal individual deductions, simplifies the marketplace-provider sales tax nexus test, sunsets the state's three tax increment financing participation programs, and makes technical changes to tax interest and TVA payment reporting. In the portion of the text provided, it does not amend Kentucky's sports wagering licensing or tax provisions.
mechanics: Section 1 (KRS 139.450): the marketplace-provider collection obligation is triggered only by more than $100,000 in sales. The 200-transaction alternative threshold is deleted, and services provided to Kentucky purchasers are expressly covered.
Section 6 (KRS 141.010(21)): for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the Internal Revenue Code is adopted as in effect on December 31, 2025.

Section 7 (KRS 141.019(2)): Kentucky still disallows federal itemized loss deductions under 26 U.S.C. 165 except wagering losses allowed under Section 165(d). Because of the updated conformity date, that carve-out now follows whatever 165(d) says as of December 31, 2025.

Section 7 also decouples from the new federal deductions for qualified tips (sec. 224), overtime (sec. 225) and passenger vehicle loan interest (sec. 163(h)(4)), and from sec. 174A R&E expensing. It limits mortgage interest to acquisition debt on one principal residence for 2026 and later.

Section 5 (KRS 154.30-030): all three state TIF participation programs sunset on the section's effective date. No new applications or amendments to existing agreements are allowed, and previously approved projects are grandfathered.

Section 2 (KRS 131.183): obsolete 2008 transition language is deleted, keeping prime plus 2% on underpayments and prime minus 2% on overpayments. Section 4 redirects TVA regional development agency reports to the Department for Local Government, which must report to the LRC by December 1.
ocd-bill/c6d93f23-fe9e-458f-a524-258d706.comparison: Iowa's SF 605, SSB 1152 and HSB 91 address state withholding on sports wagering winnings, and Colorado HB 25-1311 and Louisiana HB 639 change operator-level deductions and tax rates. Kentucky HB 757 does none of these, at least in the text provided. Its only gaming touchpoint is the existing individual income tax carve-out for wagering losses under IRC 165(d), now tied to a 2025 federal code. That makes it closer in character to the general tax omnibus bills such as Florida HB 7031 or Arizona SB 1274 than to Georgia HB 686 or Hawaii HB 2570, which are full sports-betting authorization bills.
ocd-bill/c6d93f23-fe9e-458f-a524-258d706.watch: The supplied text is cut off partway through Section 8, so check the remaining sections for any changes to Kentucky's wagering excise tax or withholding rules, and confirm whether rolling conformity to the December 31, 2025 IRC imports the federal change limiting 165(d) wagering-loss deductions for Kentucky bettors.

ocd-bill/c9641448-8cda-4c11-b482-3651838.summary: HB 904 (Acts Ch. 184) creates a licensing regime for paid fantasy contests under the Kentucky Horse Racing and Gaming Corporation, adds fixed-odds wagering on live horse racing to the KRS 138.552 excise tax, and requires licensed online gaming, sports wagering and fantasy operators to block and suspend accounts of people on a child support arrearage registry. It also adds definitions of "event contract" and "prediction market" to KRS 230.210, and lets the Lottery Corporation and the Corporation issue regulations without the Governor's signature. The supplied text is truncated partway through Section 14, so any operative provisions using the new prediction-market definitions are not visible here.
mechanics: Fixed-odds horse racing tax (Section 13, amending KRS 138.552): fixed-odds wagers on live horse racing, and parlays containing one, are taxed at the same rates as sports wagering, 9.75% at the track and 14.25% online. These wagers are carved out of adjusted gross sports wagering revenue. The proceeds go to a new purse stabilization fund (Section 12), which must be held at least 1.5 years and can be spent only to supplement live-meet purses, capped at 10% of the fund.

Fantasy contest licensing (Sections 4-11): providers must be licensed and use geolocation, and players must be 18 or older. Fees (Section 10) are: $7,500 initial and $5,000 renewal for providers already licensed as sports wagering service providers; $15,000 and $10,000 for others; $5,000 and $1,000 for providers under $50,000 in adjusted gross fantasy receipts. Existing operators may keep operating if they apply within 90 days of the regulations, which are due within 180 days. Annual CPA audit and compliance testing are required, deferred 24 months for new licensees (Section 7).

Child support registry (Section 3): the Attorney General compiles a registry of people with arrearages of $500 or more per Title IV-D case, and the Corporation passes it to operators monthly. Operators must screen applicants before opening an account and suspend matching existing accounts within 5 business days, with reinstatement within 5 business days of clearance. Knowing violations can lead to license suspension or revocation, and there is a good-faith safe harbor from private suits. Charitable gaming is exempt.

Integrity (Sections 1, 5, 8, 9): new definitions of prohibited and restricted participants (players, coaches, officials, their family members, and owners of more than 5% of a team), plus a fantasy-tampering offense. Providers must notify the Corporation of match fixing, governing-body rule breaches and illegal activity. The Corporation must investigate allegations and refer credible ones to law enforcement and sports governing bodies.

Definitions (Section 1): adds "event contract" (keyed to CEA 7 U.S.C. 1a(19)(i)), "prediction market" (any platform for event contracts or speculative positions on future events, in or out of state, including a CFTC designated contract market) and "fixed-odds wagering." It removes the horse racing exclusion from the chapter 230 definition of "sporting event" but keeps it in the tax-specific definition.

Responsible gaming and rulemaking (Sections 2, 4, 11): fantasy self-exclusion is folded into the existing program, winnings of self-excluded players are forfeited to problem-gaming charities, and a help statement is required on all marketing. Regulations no longer need the Governor's signature (new KRS Chapter 13A section), and the Corporation may not restrict fantasy contests merely by labeling them sports wagering.
ocd-bill/c9641448-8cda-4c11-b482-3651838.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639, which raises online sports wagering taxes, and CO HB 25-1311, which narrows operators' deductions, KY HB 904 leaves Kentucky's 9.75%/14.25% rates unchanged and instead applies them to a new product, fixed-odds horse racing, with that revenue reserved for purses. Its prediction-market treatment is definitional (at least in the visible text), whereas IA SF 2085 imposes a permit and a tax on event-contract markets. Its child support arrearage screening and suspension mandate for online operators has no counterpart among the listed bills, such as CO SB 131's deposit limits or the HI sports wagering bills (HB 1308, HB 2570).
ocd-bill/c9641448-8cda-4c11-b482-3651838.watch: Operators should build monthly child-support registry screening with 5-business-day suspension and reinstatement (knowing violations put the license at risk). They should also check how the new prediction-market and event-contract definitions are used in the untruncated remainder of the Act, since the CFTC-DCM language suggests the Corporation may assert jurisdiction over competing event-contract platforms.

ocd-bill/cc01aa6a-d6a5-49e4-84d2-c85231a.summary: HSB 343 (renumbered HF 1044) is Iowa's FY2025-2026 administration and regulation appropriations bill, funding agencies including the Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing (DIAL), Revenue, Management, and IPERS for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026. Its only gaming content is Section 10, which appropriates money from the gaming regulatory revolving fund to the Racing and Gaming Commission for regulating racetracks, casinos, sports wagering, and fantasy sports. Section 8 also handles DIAL fee collections under chapter 99B, which covers bingo, raffles, games of skill and chance, and social gambling. The bill makes no change to wagering tax rates, licensing standards, or operator conduct rules.
mechanics: Sec. 10 appropriates $7,448,600 and up to 53.70 FTEs from the gaming regulatory revolving fund (Iowa Code 99F.20) to the Racing and Gaming Commission within DIAL. The money funds regulation, administration, and enforcement of pari-mutuel racetracks, excursion boat gambling, gambling structures, sports wagering, and fantasy sports contests.

Sec. 8 directs DIAL to collect FY2026 license, registration, and electronic transaction fees under chapters 99B, 137C, 137D, and 137F. Fees collected for municipalities under 137F.3 go back to those municipalities. From the rest, $800,000 goes to the general fund before June 30, 2026, and DIAL keeps the remainder for enforcement, which does not revert at year end.
Sec. 8 also requires DIAL to file an annual report to the Department of Management and the Legislative Services Agency on fees billed, fees collected, and spending from the retained moneys.

Sec. 7(11) lets DIAL reallocate its general fund appropriations among its divisions, notwithstanding section 8.39. It may not move money out of labor services or workers' compensation. The gaming money in Sec. 10 is a separate revolving-fund appropriation, not part of Sec. 7.
All appropriations cover the fiscal year July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026. The last action was a committee report on 2025-05-09 renumbering the bill as HF 1044.
ocd-bill/cc01aa6a-d6a5-49e4-84d2-c85231a.comparison: Unlike the substantive sports-wagering bills on the list, such as GA HB 686 (legalization and taxation), HI HB 2570 and HB 1308 (licensing frameworks), and CO SB 131 (deposit limits), HSB 343 only funds Iowa's existing regulator and creates no new rules. It is closest in kind to KS HB 2513 and CO SB 25-107, which are also general or supplemental agency appropriations. Its gaming content is confined to the Sec. 10 Racing and Gaming Commission budget line and the 99B fee handling in Sec. 8. Nothing in the provided text touches wagering tax rates or deductions, unlike CO HB 25-1311 or LA HB 639.
ocd-bill/cc01aa6a-d6a5-49e4-84d2-c85231a.watch: Track whether the Sec. 10 Racing and Gaming Commission appropriation ($7.45M, 53.70 FTEs from the 99F.20 gaming regulatory revolving fund) or the Sec. 8 fee-retention language changes as HF 1044 moves forward, since regulator funding levels can affect assessments billed to licensees and the pace of licensing and enforcement for sports wagering and fantasy contests.

ocd-bill/cc9d69b0-bff5-4aca-9047-9656f74.summary: HB 7031E is Florida's omnibus 2026 special-session tax package, covering property tax assessment and exemption changes, sales tax holidays and exemptions, vacation-rental platform tax collection, corporate and insurance premium tax credits, and malt beverage excise taxes. Its gaming content is limited to two pari-mutuel provisions. It amends s. 551.106, F.S., to exempt certain slot machine permitholders from a license fee and to lower the tax rate on certain slot machine revenues, and it amends s. 849.086, F.S., to lower the tax cardroom operators pay on certain receipts. The bill died after being added to the Conference Report Calendar on 2026-05-28.
mechanics: s. 551.106 amendment (title, lines 89-92): certain slot machine permitholders are exempted from a specified license fee, and the tax rate on certain slot machine revenues is revised downward. The supplied text is truncated at page 30 of 66, so the affected permitholders and the new rate are not visible.
s. 849.086 amendment (title, lines 120-122): the tax paid by cardroom operators on certain receipts is revised downward. The specific rate and receipts category are not visible in the supplied text.

Section 18, effective January 1, 2027, amends s. 212.03. It requires 'advertising platforms' that offer a reservation or payment system for Florida vacation rentals to collect and remit transient rental and local option taxes. This is not gambling-advertising regulation.

Non-gaming provisions include: a property tax assessment cap of 3% for qualifying mobile home parks under new s. 193.626 (2027 roll); a home-hardening sales tax refund of up to $500 per homestead with a just value of $700,000 or less, for purchases from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2028; and the back-to-school holiday moved to July 20 through August 20.
Sports wagering, online gaming and the Seminole compact are not addressed in the visible text.
ocd-bill/cc9d69b0-bff5-4aca-9047-9656f74.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639, which increased taxation of online sports wagering, and CO HB 25-1311, which limits sports betting operators' deductions from net proceeds, FL HB 7031E does not touch sports wagering. It cuts taxes on land-based pari-mutuel slot and cardroom revenue. It is closer in form to IA SF 613 and IA SSB 1157, which bundle gaming license fees and tax rates into broader fiscal legislation. The Florida bill, however, moves only in a tax-relief direction for pari-mutuel permitholders, with no enforcement or licensing changes.
ocd-bill/cc9d69b0-bff5-4aca-9047-9656f74.watch: Although the bill is dead, an operator's counsel should watch for the s. 551.106 slot tax and fee cuts and the s. 849.086 cardroom tax cut resurfacing in a later tax package, and assess whether lowering pari-mutuel gaming taxes affects the competitive landscape or revenue-sharing dynamics under Florida's tribal gaming compact framework.

ocd-bill/d1b2c0af-badd-4312-b4e2-1b0ff51.summary: Iowa SSB 1097, a Department of Public Safety proposal later renumbered SF 395, defines "account sharing" and "proxy betting" in Code section 99F.1 and makes both criminal illegal gaming under section 725.7(1). It also adds chapter 99F to the list of chapters whose permitted activities are excepted from the illegal gaming statute. It tidies the fee-based wager delivery prohibition so that it covers things of value received outside a licensed racetrack enclosure or a gambling structure.
mechanics: "Account sharing" (new 99F.1(01)) is an agreement among two or more persons to share access, temporarily or permanently, to an account with a licensee for gambling games or sports wagering, with the purpose of concealing a person's identity.
"Proxy betting" (new 99F.1(25A)) is any wagering, including asking another person to wager, where one person bets on behalf of another with intent to hide or conceal the bettor's identity.
New 99F.15(3A) states that a person engaging in proxy betting or account sharing violates section 725.7. The prohibitions themselves are new 725.7(1)(f) and (g).

Section 725.7(1) exceptions are expanded from chapters 99B and 99D to also cover 99E and 99F. Paragraph (d) is revised to cover fee-based delivery of value received outside a licensed racetrack enclosure or outside a gambling structure.
Penalties follow the existing illegal gaming tiers by amount and offense count:
Fourth degree ($100 or less) starts as a serious misdemeanor and escalates to a class C felony on a fourth offense.
Second degree ($500 to $5,000) is a class D felony on a first offense.
First degree (over $5,000) is a class C felony, punishable by up to 10 years and a fine of $1,370 to $13,660.
No effective date is specified, so the default July 1 effective date applies. Enforcement is criminal, with no operator-side duties imposed.
ocd-bill/d1b2c0af-badd-4312-b4e2-1b0ff51.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. On its own terms, the bill is unusual because it treats proxy betting and account sharing as felony-capable crimes by the bettor and any participant, rather than as regulatory violations or grounds for account closure. It ties those crimes to the existing 725.7 tiers, which are keyed to the amount wagered and to repeat offenses.
ocd-bill/d1b2c0af-badd-4312-b4e2-1b0ff51.watch: Watch how broadly prosecutors and the Racing and Gaming Commission read the intent-to-conceal element and the 'request of another' language. Account-sharing or proxy activity detected on an operator's platform could prompt pressure for reporting, KYC, or cooperation duties, and could raise questions about voiding or voiding-and-confiscating wagers, even though the bill imposes no operator obligations.

ocd-bill/cc97988a-f12b-4b9e-b99a-0d253b5.summary: HB 1308 HD3 SD2 would legalize mobile-only sports wagering in Hawaii under a new HRS chapter regulated by the Department of Law Enforcement, with at least four operator licenses limited to qualified gaming entities and a separate supplier license. It taxes licensees at 10% of adjusted gross sports wagering receipts through a new general excise tax paragraph, section 237-13(9), in lieu of all other taxes on sports wagering, and earmarks part of that revenue for problem gambling and education. It also creates misdemeanor and felony penalties for unlicensed sports wagering and amends the chapter 712 gambling definitions (the supplied text cuts off in Section 3).
mechanics: Licensing: the Department of Law Enforcement must issue a minimum of four operator licenses (§-5), open only to a 'qualified gaming entity', meaning one already offering online sports wagering in Hawaii or in at least three US jurisdictions. The fee is $250,000 per five-year term plus cost-based processing fees. Supplier licenses cost $10,000 per five-year term. Three-year temporary licenses are available on payment of the initial fee. A universal start date must be set no later than 180 days after the effective date.

Tax: 10% of adjusted gross sports wagering receipts under new §237-13(9), which by its terms applies to both licensed operators and suppliers, on the accrual method. The receipts base is gross wagers less winnings paid, with no express deduction for promotional credits. Of collections, 7% goes to a DOH-run problem gambling special fund and 7% to education programs (§-11, §-12).

Wagering scope: mobile or digital platforms only, with no kiosks or retail terminals. Bettors must be 21 or older and physically in Hawaii unless the department signs an interstate or international agreement (§-9). Covered events include professional, collegiate (with no in-state college carve-out), amateur, Olympic, motorsports and e-sports. Youth events are excluded. Props, in-play, parlays, pools and exchange wagering are expressly included, and fantasy contests are excluded.

Operator duties (§-8, §-10): integrity monitoring for volume and odds irregularities, with reporting to the department; suspicious-bet reporting above an operator-set, department-approved threshold; department-approved house rules; '1-800-GAMBLER' in all advertising; daily receipts records; and an employee betting ban. Layoff wagers between operators are allowed. Accounts may be funded by card, bonuses or promotions, bank transfer or e-wallet.

Responsible gaming: a department-run voluntary self-exclusion program of up to lifetime duration. Operators must make reasonable efforts to stop direct marketing to excluded persons, may share the exclusion list with out-of-state affiliates, and receive the list at least quarterly.

Enforcement: civil fines up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per occurrence, applicable to non-licensees (§-13). Unlicensed wagering is a misdemeanor with a fine of at least $10,000 on a first offense, a class C felony with at least $50,000 on a second, and a class B felony with at least $100,000 on a third or later offense (§-14).
ocd-bill/cc97988a-f12b-4b9e-b99a-0d253b5.comparison: Like GA HB 686, this is a ground-up legalization act, but Hawaii's version is mobile-only with no retail or tribal/casino tether. It sets a license floor rather than a cap, and access is gated by prior multi-state operating experience. Its 10% rate matches the Colorado rate referenced in CO HB 25-1311, but Hawaii's base already allows deduction only of winnings paid, avoiding the promotional-deduction fight in Colorado.
