It is well below the rate-hike direction in LA HB 639. Unlike AR HB 1861, which focuses on criminalizing illegal online operators, Hawaii pairs legalization with an escalating felony ladder. It also lacks the deposit-frequency and other consumer-protection limits in CO SB 131.
ocd-bill/cc97988a-f12b-4b9e-b99a-0d253b5.watch: Watch whether the bill survives conference after the discharge of House conferees, and whether the drafting that extends the 10% tax to suppliers and the generic 'subject to federal income tax' winnings deduction are fixed. Also watch the department's rulemaking on temporary licenses, the tight 180-day universal start date and the operator-set suspicious-bet threshold.

ocd-bill/dcfd7170-38ca-4826-8f39-31de446.summary: Louisiana Senate Resolution 178 urges and requests the Louisiana Department of Health to study how to modernize the state's problem gambling prevention and education efforts, with a focus on youth, college-age populations and young adults. It is a non-binding simple resolution: it creates no regulatory obligations, but it asks LDH to deliver a written report with findings and recommendations by February 1, 2027.
mechanics: LDH is urged to study age-appropriate educational resources and curriculum covering gambling-related harms, financial literacy, decision-making, online gaming environments and responsible behavior.
LDH is urged to examine voluntary digital tools and mobile resources for prevention, self-assessment, awareness, early intervention and connection to behavioral health and recovery services.
LDH is to consult with the Department of Education, the Board of Regents, colleges and universities, behavioral health providers, community organizations, researchers and other stakeholders.
A written report is due to the Senate and the David R. Poynter Legislative Research Library under R.S. 24:771 and 772 no later than February 1, 2027.
There are no taxes, fees, operator mandates or enforcement provisions; the whereas clauses cite expanded legal sports wagering and youth exposure through advertising, social media and mobile apps.
ocd-bill/dcfd7170-38ca-4826-8f39-31de446.comparison: Unlike the Hawaii sports wagering bills (HB 2570 and HB 1308), SR 178 does not legalize anything or impose any tax. Those bills would create licensing regimes and a Problem Gambling fund, while this resolution only commissions a study. It is also far softer than Colorado SB 131, which imposes direct operator limits such as a cap of 6 deposits per gaming day. SR 178 addresses problem gambling purely through public-health education and voluntary tools, and it places no obligations on licensees.
ocd-bill/dcfd7170-38ca-4826-8f39-31de446.watch: Watch the February 1, 2027 LDH report for recommendations that could later become legislation, such as youth-focused advertising restrictions, mandated operator funding for prevention programs or required integration with self-assessment and referral tools.

ocd-bill/df5e955e-f2fc-4ae1-a0dd-bbd6b51.summary: HF 2503 is an omnibus Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing bill whose Division I amends Iowa's gambling statutes (chapters 99D and 99F). It raises the cap on total expense reimbursements for Racing and Gaming Commission members from $30,000 to $70,000 per year, and extends the existing lifetime ban for 99F.15(4) felony offenders and for persons twice convicted of unlawful betting so that it covers sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering, not just excursion gambling boats and gambling structures. Divisions II and III address unrelated state building code and residential care facility matters.
mechanics: Sec. 1 (99D.5(4)): commission members keep the $10,000 annual salary, and the aggregate cap on reimbursed actual expenses rises from $30,000 to $70,000 per year for the commission.

Sec. 2 (99F.15(4)): a person committing an enumerated class D felony offense is barred for life from sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering (as defined in 99F.9), in addition to excursion gambling boats and gambling structures.
Sec. 3 (99F.15(6)(c)): two convictions for unlawful betting trigger the same expanded lifetime bar, including sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering.

Divisions II and III are non-gaming: safe room/storm shelter rule consultation moves to Homeland Security and Emergency Management, building code fees go to the licensing and regulation fund under 10A.507, and pediatric palliative residential care facilities may serve zero individuals.
No effective date is specified, so Iowa's default July 1 effective date would apply if enacted.
ocd-bill/df5e955e-f2fc-4ae1-a0dd-bbd6b51.comparison: Unlike HI HB 2570, HI HB 1308 and GA HB 686, which would build full sports wagering licensing and tax frameworks, HF 2503 makes narrow adjustments to an existing Iowa regime. It is closer to agency-housekeeping measures such as CO SB 163 and KY HB 566, which tweak regulator powers and administration. Its integrity angle, extending lifetime exclusions to sports wagering, differs from CO SB 131's consumer-protection deposit limits because it targets cheaters and unlawful bettors rather than the conduct of operators.
ocd-bill/df5e955e-f2fc-4ae1-a0dd-bbd6b51.watch: Operators should prepare to identify and block, on both retail and advance-deposit (online) sports wagering platforms, persons subject to the expanded lifetime bans under 99F.15, and should watch for commission rules or exclusion-list procedures setting out how that compliance will be enforced.

ocd-bill/df7fd551-ab49-4070-bfe8-bfb6dd7.summary: SB 135 amends R.S. 27:625(G)(2) and (8) to change how the state treasurer distributes Louisiana's tax on sports wagering net gaming proceeds collected under Subsection B between two dedicated funds. As engrossed, both provisions credit 25% of Subsection B collections, capped at $20 million, to the Louisiana Early Childhood Education Fund (R.S. 17:407.30) and to the Supporting Programs, Opportunities, Resources, and Teams (SPORT) Fund (R.S. 17:1792). It does not change the tax rate or any operator obligation.
mechanics: Amends R.S. 27:625(G)(2): 25% of Subsection B collections, 'not to exceed twenty million dollars,' goes to the Louisiana Early Childhood Education Fund. The digest describes this as tied to net mobile sports wagering proceeds.
Amends R.S. 27:625(G)(8): adds a $20 million cap on the 25% share of Subsection B collections credited to the SPORT Fund, which was previously uncapped per the digest.
Distributions apply each fiscal year only after the Subsection D requirements are met.
Senate Finance amendments dropped an earlier version that guaranteed the Early Childhood fund the greater of 25% or $20 million, removing that floor.
Effective July 1, 2027, moved from July 1, 2026 by committee amendment. Passed the Senate and on 2026-05-18 was referred to the House Committee on Administration of Criminal Justice.
ocd-bill/df7fd551-ab49-4070-bfe8-bfb6dd7.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. This bill is unusual because it only reallocates already-collected sports wagering tax revenue between two education and youth funds, with no change to rates, licensing or conduct rules. The digest also conflicts with the bill text: it says the $20 million cap on the Early Childhood fund is removed, yet the visible engrossed text keeps the cap. The lost strikethrough formatting makes the final effect on that fund uncertain.
ocd-bill/df7fd551-ab49-4070-bfe8-bfb6dd7.watch: The bill does not touch operator tax rates as engrossed, but in the House it is a vehicle on R.S. 27:625, so watch for amendments that raise the Subsection B rate or change the deductions behind net gaming proceeds to fund these capped dedications.

ocd-bill/e0185e15-d7a8-4bad-9c24-5237e5c.summary: Iowa HSB 586 (renumbered HF 2503) is a Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing omnibus bill whose Division I gives the Racing and Gaming Commission express cease-and-desist and injunctive authority against unlicensed pari-mutuel, advance deposit wagering, internet fantasy sports, casino gaming, sports wagering and illegal sweepstakes operators. It also extends existing lifetime bans for gambling-related felonies and repeat unlawful betting to cover sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering, and removes the $30,000 annual cap on commissioner expense reimbursement. Divisions II and III make unrelated changes to the state building code and residential care facility rules.
mechanics: Sec. 1 (99D.5(4)): strikes the $30,000-per-year aggregate cap on reimbursement of commissioners' actual expenses; the $10,000 salary is unchanged.

Secs. 2-4 (99D.7(25), 99E.3(2)(f), 99F.4(13)): add explicit authority to issue cease and desist orders and obtain injunctive relief against anyone offering pari-mutuel or advance deposit wagering, internet fantasy sports contests, or games of chance, gambling, sports wagering or illegal sweepstakes in Iowa without a commission license. Under 99F the order can also issue against anyone not 'otherwise being specifically authorized by law.'

Sec. 5 (99F.15(4)): persons committing the listed class 'D' felony acts are now barred for life from sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering (as defined in 99F.9), in addition to the existing bar from excursion gambling boats and gambling structures.
Sec. 6 (99F.15(6)(c)): two convictions for unlawful betting trigger the same lifetime bar, now extended to sports wagering and advance deposit sports wagering.

Divisions II-III (non-gaming): building code fees are redirected to the licensing and regulation fund (103A.23), the safe room rules consultation shifts to homeland security and emergency management (103A.8C), and pediatric palliative residential care facilities may serve zero individuals (135C.2(6)).
No effective date provision appears in the text, so Iowa's default July 1 effective date would presumably apply.
ocd-bill/e0185e15-d7a8-4bad-9c24-5237e5c.comparison: Unlike CA AB 831, which defines and prohibits specific sweepstakes practices, Iowa's bill does not define 'illegal sweepstakes.' Instead it gives the regulator a summary enforcement tool, cease and desist orders, against unlicensed sweepstakes, sports wagering and fantasy operators, an administrative route rather than new substantive prohibitions. It resembles the regulator-housekeeping approach of CO SB 163 and KY HB 566, which adjust commission powers and jurisdiction, but Iowa's changes are narrower: no tax, licensing-fee or consumer-protection changes like those in CO HB 25-1311 or CO SB 131. It also contrasts with the legalization frameworks in GA HB 686 and HI HB 2570/HB 1308, since Iowa already has legal sports wagering and is simply tightening enforcement and integrity sanctions.
ocd-bill/e0185e15-d7a8-4bad-9c24-5237e5c.watch: Operators should watch how the commission uses its new cease-and-desist power under 99F.4(13), particularly against sweepstakes, social or prediction-style products it may treat as unlicensed 'gambling' or 'sports wagering,' and should ensure exclusion systems can implement the expanded lifetime sports wagering bans under 99F.15.

ocd-bill/e0a1e4f3-db02-4ba8-a9d4-8865926.summary: HB 566 (Acts Ch. 124, with an emergency clause) restructures the governance, funding and oversight of the Kentucky Horse Racing and Gaming Corporation (KHRGC), Kentucky's regulator for racing, pari-mutuel wagering, sports wagering and, from July 1, 2025, charitable gaming. It expands the board, shifts removal of the president from the Governor to the board, changes the audit cycle, and makes the corporation self-funded after FY2025-26. It also adds pari-mutuel definitions for unclaimed winning tickets and unredeemed vouchers, which are presumed abandoned under Section 42 of the Act.
mechanics: Board grows from 15 to 17 gubernatorial appointees (Sec. 4, KRS 230.227). A third charitable gaming seat and a quarter horse industry seat are added, alongside three gaming-industry experts and one at-large member with no financial interest. Staggered 2- and 3-year initial terms begin July 1, 2026.

The word "plenary" is struck from the corporation's rulemaking power over horse racing, sports wagering and charitable gaming (Sec. 2, KRS 230.215(2)). The board now "recommends" rather than promulgates regulations, and the corporation keeps final promulgation authority (Secs. 4 and 6).

New KRS 230.225(13)(d) bars the corporation from exercising jurisdiction over matters "within the exclusive national authority of entities designated by the laws of the United States." New (13)(c) bars it from prohibiting charitable games in use as of July 1, 2025 without General Assembly action.

Funding and audits (Sec. 3, KRS 230.225): after FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 appropriations are transferred, the corporation must be self-sustaining with no general fund money. The Auditor of Public Accounts audits once every four years and a qualified outside auditor audits in the other years, starting with FY2026-27.

President (Sec. 5, KRS 230.230): the Governor appoints from a board list of up to three names, the board may remove the president, and the budget becomes annual instead of biennial. CFO qualifications are revised to a relevant bachelor's degree plus 10 years of finance and accounting experience, including 5 in senior management; the CPA option is dropped.

New definitions in Sec. 1 (KRS 230.210): "Kentucky resident" for advance deposit wagering accounts, a separate Kentucky quarter horse purse fund, "proof of wagers," "unclaimed pari-mutuel winning ticket" and "unredeemed pari-mutuel voucher." The corporation must annually evaluate how unredeemed voucher funds are allocated (KRS 230.225(5)(k)).
ocd-bill/e0a1e4f3-db02-4ba8-a9d4-8865926.comparison: Like CO SB 163, which reallocates licensing duties between Colorado's gaming commission and division, HB 566 is a regulator-governance bill rather than a tax or product bill; it does not change sports wagering tax rates or licensing terms as GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570 would. It contrasts with KS SB 356, which affirmatively grants rulemaking authority for sports wagering, because HB 566 instead trims the KHRGC's language to remove "plenary" power. Its express carve-out for matters within exclusive federal authority is unusual among the listed bills, and Iowa's SF 2085 takes the opposite approach to federally traded event contracts by requiring a state permit and tax.
ocd-bill/e0a1e4f3-db02-4ba8-a9d4-8865926.watch: Watch three things: how the self-funding mandate drives new fees or assessments on sports wagering licensees and service providers; whether the removal of "plenary" rulemaking authority invites challenges to KHRGC regulations; and whether KRS 230.225(13)(d) is invoked to disclaim state jurisdiction over CFTC-regulated event contracts (the text provided is truncated after Section 6, so Sections 10, 11, 14 and 42 could not be reviewed).

ocd-bill/e25e4538-bf67-46ea-abf0-309b050.summary: SF 660 does not change how sports wagering is taxed, licensed or conducted in Iowa; it spends money from the sports wagering receipts fund (Iowa Code 8.57I). It adds two ongoing claims on the fund and four one-time FY2025-26 appropriations. It also creates a new Iowa major events and tourism grant program (new chapter 15G) and repeals the sports tourism marketing fund (15F.403), moving that fund's balance into the new program.
mechanics: Sec. 1 amends 8.57I(3) to make a standing annual appropriation of $8 million from the sports wagering receipts fund to the public safety equipment fund (80.48), starting FY2025-26, exempt from the reporting rules in subsections 4 and 5.

Sec. 2 adds 8.57I(3A): from FY2026-27, the fund must top up the length of service award program grant fund (100B.52) to a $1.5 million balance each July 1. This takes effect only if HF 1002 is enacted (Sec. 8) and is repealed July 1, 2030.

Secs. 3-6 make one-time FY2025-26 appropriations from the fund: $14 million for education support personnel pay, split among school districts by budget enrollment and effective on enactment (Sec. 7); $5 million for the special education division; $4 million to the film production incentive fund, contingent on SF 657; and $4 million to the new major events and tourism fund.

Division II creates chapter 15G. The economic development authority board may give grants to Iowa nonprofit economic development and tourism entities for bid, hosting, sanctioning and operating costs of athletic contests, conventions and music or art festivals. Recipients must put up a 50% match, administration is capped at 5% of the fund, and funding decisions are exempt from chapter 17A.

Division III narrows chapter 15F to an infrastructure-only program and repeals the sports tourism marketing fund (15F.403), transferring its remaining balance to the 15G fund (Sec. 23). Entities cannot receive assistance under both programs.
ocd-bill/e25e4538-bf67-46ea-abf0-309b050.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. What stands out is that the title says the bill relates to sports wagering, yet it contains nothing on operators, tax rates, licensing or wagering conduct. Its only link to wagering is using the 8.57I receipts fund as a funding source. The notable step is turning a fund previously spent 'as directed by the general assembly' into a source of permanent and formula-driven claims: the $8 million yearly public safety appropriation and the uncapped length of service award top-up.
ocd-bill/e25e4538-bf67-46ea-abf0-309b050.watch: The new standing claims on the sports wagering receipts fund (the $8 million yearly public safety appropriation and the open-ended length of service award top-up) make the state more dependent on sports wagering revenue, which could add pressure in future sessions to raise the wagering tax or fees if receipts fall short.

ocd-bill/e4aaa11c-4493-4248-9bae-458500b.summary: Act 48 of 2026 adds seven gambling-related crimes to the list of predicate offenses for "racketeering activity" in Louisiana's racketeering statute, R.S. 15:1352(A). Committing, attempting, conspiring to commit, or soliciting, coercing or intimidating someone to commit any of these offenses can now support a racketeering charge. The listed offenses include general gambling, computer gambling, electronic sweepstakes devices, prohibited-player wagering and bribery of sports participants.
mechanics: Enacts R.S. 15:1352(A)(89)-(95), adding predicates: R.S. 14:90 (Gambling), 14:90.2 (Gambling in public), 14:90.3 (Gambling by computer), 14:90.6 (Gambling or wagering at cockfights), 14:90.7 (Gambling by electronic sweepstakes device), 14:90.8 (Unlawful wagering; prohibited player), and 14:118.1 (Bribery of sports participants).
Existing 1352(A) language applies, so attempt, conspiracy, solicitation, coercion and intimidation to commit any listed crime also count as racketeering activity.
Section 2 directs the Louisiana Law Institute to renumber the new entries so the list stays in alphabetical order.
No special effective date is stated in the text, so Louisiana's default effective date for regular-session acts would apply.
The Act creates no new standalone offense or penalty. It brings the existing gambling crimes into the reach of the Racketeering Chapter's existing penalties and remedies.
ocd-bill/e4aaa11c-4493-4248-9bae-458500b.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. What is unusual is the approach. Rather than changing licensing or creating new gambling crimes, the Act uses racketeering law to raise the stakes for illegal gambling. It covers unlicensed online gambling, sweepstakes devices, prohibited-player wagering under R.S. 14:90.8 and sports-participant bribery, which together reach both illegal-market and integrity misconduct.
ocd-bill/e4aaa11c-4493-4248-9bae-458500b.watch: Operators should check how R.S. 14:90.8 (prohibited-player wagering) and 14:118.1 (sports bribery) interact with their compliance obligations, because a pattern of these offenses, including conspiracy or solicitation by employees or affiliates, can now support racketeering charges and the forfeiture exposure that comes with them.

ocd-bill/e7b475a0-923a-4772-9233-8753233.summary: SF 621 creates a new Iowa major events and tourism program and fund (new Code ch. 15G) under the Economic Development Authority to award grants to Iowa nonprofit economic-development/tourism entities that bid for and host major events, and appropriates $15 million from the sports wagering receipts fund (section 8.57I) for FY 2025-26 to seed it. It also repeals the sports tourism marketing program fund (section 15F.403), narrows section 15F.401 to an infrastructure-only program, and sweeps remaining marketing-fund balances into the new fund. Sports betting matters here only as the revenue source; the bill does not touch wagering regulation, taxes, or licensing.
mechanics: Sec. 5 appropriates $15,000,000 from the sports wagering receipts fund (section 8.57I) to the new Iowa major events and tourism fund for FY beginning July 1, 2025.

Eligible 'entity' is an Iowa nonprofit established to promote economic development and tourism; 'event' means a tourism-oriented athletic contest, convention, music festival, or art festival (15G.101).

Grants may cover bid/application costs and planning or conduct costs, including hosting, sanctioning, participation, operational, and bid fees; applicants must show matching funds of at least 50% of the award (15G.102, 15G.103(4)(b)).

EDA board makes final funding decisions, exempt from chapter 17A; applications remain eligible for two years; administrative costs are capped at 5% of the fund; encumbered funds must be disbursed within five years or revert (15G.103-.104).
Recipients under the new program are barred from the sports tourism infrastructure program under ch. 15F, subchapter IV (15G.104(2)(b)).

Division III repeals section 15F.403 (sports tourism marketing program fund), removes the $500,000-per-year marketing award cap language, bars use of infrastructure funds to reimburse completed projects, and transfers remaining marketing-fund moneys to the new fund (Secs. 6-16).
ocd-bill/e7b475a0-923a-4772-9233-8753233.comparison: Unlike CO SB 131, which directly regulates internet sports betting operators (deposit limits and related consumer protections), and CA AB 831, which addresses sweepstakes and contest practices, IA SF 621 imposes no obligations on operators at all. Its only connection to wagering is that it draws down Iowa's sports wagering receipts fund, the account fed by sports betting tax revenue, to finance event-hosting grants. That makes it an appropriations and economic-development bill, not a gaming regulation bill.
ocd-bill/e7b475a0-923a-4772-9233-8753233.watch: Track whether the $15 million draw on the sports wagering receipts fund, now moving as SF 640, signals legislative appetite to treat sports-betting tax revenue as a recurring source for tourism spending, which could feed future pressure to raise operator tax rates or reallocate the fund.

ocd-bill/e99951d0-7c05-4acd-8129-5bcd72f.summary: Act 298 raises Louisiana's tax on net gaming proceeds from online sports wagering (website or mobile app) from 15% to 21.5% under R.S. 27:625(B), leaving retail wagering through a sports wagering mechanism untouched. It redirects 25% of online sports wagering tax collections to a new Supporting Programs, Opportunities, Resources, and Teams (SPORTS) Fund for Division I university athletic departments and 3% to the Louisiana Postsecondary Inclusive Education Fund, with the remainder going to the state general fund. Despite the digest title, the enrolled text contains no video poker provisions.
mechanics: R.S. 27:625(B): online sports wagering tax rises from 15% to 21.5% of net gaming proceeds; electronic wagering through an in-person sports wagering mechanism is expressly excluded.
R.S. 27:625(G)(8): 25% of Subsection B collections go to the new SPORTS Fund (R.S. 17:1792), after Subsection D obligations are met.
R.S. 27:625(G)(9)-(10): 3% goes to the Louisiana Postsecondary Inclusive Education Fund (R.S. 17:3138.11), and any remainder goes to the state general fund.

R.S. 17:1792: Board of Regents distributes SPORTS Fund money equally among public universities in FBS and FCS conferences. Permitted uses are scholarships, insurance, medical coverage, facility enhancements, litigation settlement fees and Alston awards, and the money may not supplant other awards.
The text states no separate effective date or change to deductions, licensing or enforcement. The fiscal note estimates about +$34.7 million in revenue.
ocd-bill/e99951d0-7c05-4acd-8129-5bcd72f.comparison: Colorado HB 25-1311 raises effective tax by restricting operators' deductions against the existing 10% rate, whereas Louisiana HB 639 simply raises the headline online rate by 6.5 points and leaves the deduction base alone. Iowa SF 613 and SSB 1157 combine tax rate and license fee changes with gambling enforcement and dedicate revenue to tourism and major events; Louisiana instead earmarks a fixed share to college athletics, including Alston awards and litigation settlement costs. Hawaii HB 1308 and HB 2570 and Georgia HB 686 would legalize and tax sports betting from scratch, while Iowa SF 605 deals only with winnings withholding.
ocd-bill/e99951d0-7c05-4acd-8129-5bcd72f.watch: Operators should watch the split between online and retail rates and the definition of "sports wagering mechanism" in 27:625(B), and should expect the college-athletics earmark to create a constituency for further online rate increases.

ocd-bill/e79301a0-4505-4722-bce9-3fa8fe4.summary: SB 26-131 layers consumer-protection limits onto Colorado's existing sports betting regime. It bans solicitation push notifications, caps deposits at six per gaming day, prohibits credit card funding, and restricts advertising aimed at under-21 audiences. It also requires annual transactional data submissions, tightens integrity reporting to sports governing bodies, and lets leagues petition to restrict any type of wager on their events.
mechanics: Online operators may not send push notifications, including texts shown when the app is not open, that solicit bets or deposits (44-30-1501(8.7), 44-30-1506(8)(b)). Deposits are capped at six per individual per operator-defined 24-hour gaming day (1506(8)(a)(II)).

Accepting credit card deposits, directly or indirectly (including via accounts funded by a credit card), is unlawful under 44-30-1511(1)(d). Violations carry a monetary penalty of up to $25,000, in addition to or instead of suspension or revocation (44-30-524(1)(b)(III)).

New 44-30-1506.5 bars operators and their marketing affiliates (paid promoters, excluding broadcasters) from targeting under-21s or creating content clearly meant for them. It also bars advertising on any media whose audience is reasonably expected to be majority under-21, with an exception for public venues where attendee demographics cannot be determined.

Integrity reports under 1506(5)(a)(II)-(III) must now be made 'as soon as practicable' and sent simultaneously to the relevant sports governing body. The division and operators must use 'reasonable efforts' to cooperate with league investigations, replacing the earlier 'good and sufficient reason' standard. Leagues may petition the commission to restrict, limit, or exclude any type of wager on their events, no longer only single-player-outcome bets (1505(7)).

Starting February 1, 2028, and every February 1 after, online operators must submit all transactional data and metrics for the prior year, redacted of PII and exempt from CORA. The division publishes a compiled report by January 1, 2029 and every three years after (44-30-1507.5).

The act takes effect August 12, 2026 (assuming May 13 adjournment), unless a referendum petition is filed, and applies to conduct and agreements on or after that date. It also appropriates $124,623 and 0.5 FTE to the Department of Law, and requires the sports betting fund's water plan transfer to be no less than the prior year's (1509(2)(e)).
ocd-bill/e79301a0-4505-4722-bce9-3fa8fe4.comparison: Unlike the authorization bills listed (GA HB 686, HI HB 2570 and HB 1308), which create licensing and tax frameworks for new markets, Colorado's SB 131 imposes operational restrictions on a mature legal market. It also differs from tax-focused measures such as LA HB 639 and enforcement-against-illegal-operators bills such as AR HB 1861, because it targets licensed operators' marketing, payment, and engagement practices. Its combination of a hard deposit-frequency cap, a solicitation push-notification ban, and a credit card prohibition with a specific $25,000 penalty is unusual among the listed bills, as is mandatory annual data disclosure feeding a public triennial report.
ocd-bill/e79301a0-4505-4722-bce9-3fa8fe4.watch: Operators should watch how the commission interprets several open provisions: the scope of 'relating to the solicitation of bets or deposits' for push notifications, 'indirectly' funded credit card deposits (such as e-wallets or PayPal backed by cards), affiliate liability under the majority-under-21 audience test, and the breadth of 'all transactional data and metrics,' since these will drive compliance costs from August 12, 2026 onward.

ocd-bill/eadf67a9-7f87-4f60-b071-0ce3871.summary: SSB 1106 (renumbered SF 465) is an Iowa Economic Development Authority and Iowa Finance Authority agency bill. It restructures review committees, repeals the brownfield redevelopment program and advisory council, and tightens historic preservation tax credit timelines. It also abolishes the title guaranty board and consolidates several arts and culture programs into a new arts and culture enhancement fund. Its only gaming touchpoint is Sec. 36, which redirects a fixed $520,000 annual appropriation of gaming tax revenue under Iowa Code section 99F.11 into that new fund.
mechanics: Sec. 36 amends section 99F.11(4)(d)(1), the distribution of state wagering tax receipts: the $520,000 appropriated each fiscal year to IEDA, previously split between operational support grants and community cultural grants, is redirected to the arts and culture enhancement fund under new section 15.436.

Sec. 32 rewrites section 15.436 to create a non-reverting arts and culture enhancement fund. Interest stays in the fund. Permitted uses include support for arts organizations, rural access, and film and television promotion. Sec. 38 transfers balances from the Iowa great places fund and the cultural trust fund and grant account, and Sec. 37 repeals the underlying programs.

Sec. 15 amends section 15F.402: review of sports tourism marketing and infrastructure program applications moves from five IEDA board members to a director-appointed committee with relevant expertise. The program concerns sports events tourism, not wagering.

Division III repeals section 15F.106, the requirement that recipients of both Vision Iowa and community attraction and tourism assistance pay at least 50% of employee health insurance, with retroactive applicability (Sec. 13).

Division V sets historic preservation credit timelines: commencement within one year of the registration date and completion within three calendar years, with discretionary 12-month extensions. It adds a single-family dwelling exclusion and lets IEDA exceed the $45 million annual cap by up to 20% for projects eligible for $10 million or more in credits, beginning FY2026, with the excess counted against the next year's cap.
ocd-bill/eadf67a9-7f87-4f60-b071-0ce3871.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639, which changes online sports wagering and video poker tax rates and dedicates gaming revenue, SSB 1106 changes no gaming tax rate. It only re-labels the destination of an existing $520,000 carve-out from Iowa's 99F wagering tax. It resembles the omnibus fiscal vehicles CO SB 25-107 and FL HB 7031, which touch gaming or tourism revenue only in passing. It shares none of the operator-facing provisions in CO HB 25-1311 (deductions), CO SB 131 (deposit limits), or the HI and GA authorization bills.
ocd-bill/eadf67a9-7f87-4f60-b071-0ce3871.watch: Operators should note only that Sec. 36 reopens section 99F.11 revenue distributions in a moving vehicle, and watch for amendments that change the distribution list, since a reopened section can draw rate or allocation changes affecting sports wagering receipts.

ocd-bill/ee984555-853e-4199-b991-b46d6a8.summary: SB 451 (Chapter 584, Statutes of 2025) clarifies that the California Department of Justice may investigate suspected criminal violations of the Penal Code's gambling prohibitions (lotteries, banned card and dice games, slot machines, and others) even when they occur outside a licensed gambling establishment and whether or not a licensee is involved. It also expands the existing major league sports raffle program so eligible nonprofits can run a raffle at a championship game, provided the game is held at the affiliated team's designated home venue.
mechanics: Enforcement: confirms DOJ authority under the Gambling Control Act to investigate suspected violations of the enumerated Penal Code gambling prohibitions outside licensed gambling establishments, irrespective of whether the suspected violation involves licensees.

Major league sports raffles: existing law allows these only at home games, with 50% of gross ticket receipts going to beneficial or charitable purposes, 50% to the winner, and winners chosen by manual draw.
The bill adds championship games as a permitted raffle occasion, but only if the game is held at the designated venue where the affiliated team plays its home games.
The existing limit of one major league sports raffle per home game remains. The abstract does not say how that limit applies to championship games.
Because the bill expands provisions that reduce the constitutional 90% charitable-receipts requirement, it required a two-thirds vote of each house. The abstract's '23 vote' is a rendering of 2/3.
The bill also makes technical and conforming changes. Only the official abstract was available, not the full text, so section numbers cannot be cited.
ocd-bill/ee984555-853e-4199-b991-b46d6a8.comparison: Unlike GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570, which would authorize and tax sports wagering, SB 451 leaves California's ban on sports betting in place. It only marginally expands a charitable raffle tied to major league sports events. Its enforcement clarification is closest to AR HB 1861, but Arkansas creates a new felony for illegal online casino and sports betting operations, while California only confirms DOJ's investigative reach beyond licensed card rooms. None of the listed bills addresses charitable sports raffles, which makes the championship-game expansion unusual.
ocd-bill/ee984555-853e-4199-b991-b46d6a8.watch: Watch how DOJ uses its confirmed authority to investigate gambling activity outside licensed establishments, whatever the licensee involvement, because it could support investigations of unlicensed or alternative gaming products offered to Californians, including by companies that hold no California license.

ocd-bill/f00dac3d-8ef4-4cd3-b99d-319d450.summary: SSB 1157 (renumbered SF 613) raises Iowa's sports wagering tax on net receipts from 6.75% to 9%. It replaces the graduated casino adjusted gross receipts tax with flat rates and doubles the casino annual license fee. It also shifts DCI gaming enforcement funding from licensee regulatory fees to an off-the-top credit of AGR tax, and redirects sports wagering receipts to public safety equipment ($8M a year) and a new $15M Iowa Major Events and Tourism Fund.
mechanics: Sports wagering tax under Iowa Code 99F.11(5)(a) rises from 6.75% to 9% of sports wagering net receipts (Sec. 15); Division I takes effect January 1, 2026 (Sec. 16).

The casino AGR tax drops the 5% (first $1M) and 10% (next $2M) tiers and the variable racetrack rates; it becomes a flat 22% for excursion boats and gambling structures and 24.125% for racetrack enclosures, whether or not they hold a table games license (Secs. 11-12).
The annual license fee for excursion gambling boats and gambling structures doubles from $5 to $10 per person of capacity (Sec. 6).

The DCI enforcement-cost component of the 99D.14 and 99F.10 regulatory fees is struck (Secs. 3-10). From FY2026-27, AGR tax is instead credited to the gaming enforcement revolving fund up to the amount appropriated to DPS, before the remainder goes to the rebuild Iowa infrastructure fund (Sec. 14). Internet fantasy sports background-check fees under 99E.4(4) are unchanged.

Beginning FY2026-27, $8M a year is appropriated from the sports wagering receipts fund to the public safety equipment fund (Sec. 1). A one-time $15M for FY2025-26 goes to the new Iowa Major Events and Tourism Fund under new chapter 15G (Sec. 21).

The new 15G program gives grants to Iowa nonprofits for bid, hosting and sanctioning costs of major events, with a 50% match requirement and a 5% administrative cap (Secs. 17-20). The sports tourism marketing fund (15F.403) is repealed and its balance transferred to the new fund (Secs. 31-32).
ocd-bill/f00dac3d-8ef4-4cd3-b99d-319d450.comparison: Like LA HB 639, which raises Louisiana's online sports wagering tax and dedicates gaming revenue, SSB 1157 combines a sports betting rate increase with earmarks of the proceeds. Its 9% rate on net receipts remains low by national standards. CO HB 25-1311 takes a different route to more revenue: it keeps Colorado's 10% rate but narrows the deductions operators can take in calculating net proceeds, whereas Iowa raises the headline rate and leaves the net receipts base untouched. Unlike GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570, which would legalize and build sports wagering regimes from scratch, Iowa's bill adjusts an existing market and pairs the sports tax change with a flattening of land-based casino AGR taxes that eliminates the low-revenue tiers.
ocd-bill/f00dac3d-8ef4-4cd3-b99d-319d450.watch: Operators should watch whether the 9% rate survives in SF 613 or is raised further, and how a January 1, 2026 effective date applies to a tax imposed on receipts 'each fiscal year', which could mean mid-year proration or partial-year compliance issues. Casino-affiliated licensees should also watch the loss of the 5%/10% AGR tiers and the doubled per-capacity license fee.
